stories.title: Morning fog advisory in London and region
stories.summary: Morning fog advisory in London and region CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: New CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 11:50 AM | Last Updated: Just now
Sunshine and temperatures of 23 C expected in the afternoon
Environment Canada has issued a fog advisory for the London region Friday morning.
The yellow-level advisory, which is the weather agency's lowest risk warning, covers London, Parkhill and Eastern Middlesex County.
Londoners May notice areas of dense fog and near-zero visibility, Environment Canada said on its website, adding that travel "will likely be hazardous in some locations."
The agency is recommending Londoners allow extra time to reach their destinations this morning.
Fog is expected to dissipate later this morning, revealing sunshine with a high of 23 C.
The sun is expected to continue into the weekend with highs of 27 C on both Saturday and Sunday.

stories.title: One divisive city council era. Two would-be comebacks. Will London voters care?
stories.summary: Two members of the so-called Fontana 8 voting bloc from nearly a generation ago are trying to win back their old seats in the fall civic election.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
In something of a blast from the past, two former London politicians who were part of an infamous voting bloc on city council are trying for comebacks in the fall civic election.

The question is, will the notoriety of the political past sink their hoped-for resurrection in the Oct. 26 vote?

Or, do voters have bigger issues on their minds – never mind enough recall to think back to an often-acrimonious era – for that to matter?

One of the two candidate says he’s unapologetic for his political record, and at least one prominent political observer says it’s not so clear past baggage will be a key factor for voters.

Among the 69 candidates running for election in London’s 14 ward council races are the two ex-politicians – Stephen Orser and Denise Brown – seeking their old seats back in Wards 4 and 11, respectively.

Orser and Brown were part of the so-called Fontana 8, a voting bloc of eight council members including then-mayor Joe Fontana between 2010 and 2014.

The spectre of a comeback has drawn the attention and ire of another former city councillor, Stephen Turner, who defeated Brown in 2014 and in a social media post said he hopes to see the former Fontana 8 members “swiftly” defeated at the ballot box.

“It’s disappointing to see Fontana 8 folks popping their heads back up for this election. That era was London politics at its worst,” he wrote.

With a voting majority on the 15-member council, the Fontana 8 dominated in its day – pushing through much of Fontana’s agenda.

Gord Hume, a former council member who bowed out of civic politics as the Fontana 8 era began, said the divide on that council occurred quickly and got bitter over the life of its term.

“(That) council certainly split very early in that term into a group of five, six who were more socially driven, and then seven or eight who were more business-driven coalesced around Fontana. There was a definite chasm on council,” said Hume, now a municipal consultant.

Kirsten Krose promises traffic plan, city hall dashboard in mayoral platform

Nominations close with 110 candidates in London civic election

“The seven not in the bloc were increasingly frustrated because most of their ideas and motions and proposals were shot down. Not always for the best of reasons, but just because they could . . . and because of that, debate deteriorated.

“It was not civil in any way whatsoever, and a lot of people became embittered and that went out into the community,” Hume said.

Council’s standing committees, the first point of contact with politicians for all issues before they go to council for final decisions, were both chaired by and their memberships dominated by Fontana 8 members.

The acrimony boiled over after Fontana was criminally charged with fraud, breach of trust by a public official and uttering forged documents.

A first attempt at a council motion to ask Fontana to step aside was shot down before even being tabled.

A second go at it failed in an 8-5 vote, with Fontana sitting it out and once council member absent.

“That event caused a huge chasm in the community, and they (the public) lost confidence in the council. The public was angry . . . distaste for that council was palpable,” Hume said, noting many Londoners in 2014 were simply of a mood to vote councillors out.

Fontana would resign as mayor a few months ahead of the 2014 election, which brought a political sea change with an astounding 11 new members elected to council’s 15 seats – “a revolution,” as Hume put it.

Brown and Orser were booted from office. So was Paul Van Meerbergen, who was also part of the Fontana 8. He was subsequently elected in 2018 and has remained on council since as the Ward 10 representative.

Orser has run in every election as a candidate in Ward 4 since 2014, but Brown mounted her comeback bid last week, ON the last day for candidates to file their nomination papers for this fall’s contest.

For all the past drama, Hume notes it was more than decade ago and says unless rival candidates or attentive voters raise it, it’s “history” that many Londoners either won’t remember or which could be overshadowed by other issues.

“Some of those views would have moderated in the (10-plus) years since, and everybody has the right to change their minds. Everybody has the right to get fresh thinking,” he said.

“I guess what would be interesting is, what are their platforms this time? What are they presenting as their vision for the city?”

Thursday, Orser told The Free Press he’s unapologetic. He takes credit for helping to form the bloc and said it contributed to achieving many of his goals for Ward 4, including bringing new highrise development to his district and cracking down on crime in the area.

“We organized a voting bloc for the purpose of pushing London forward,” he said, adding other councils have also had their own blocs. “It’s no different than any political party.”

Orser said hands-on experience is needed to handle “out of control” problems such as homelessness and open drug use, which he argues today’s council “has dropped the ball on.” He applauds Brown as “a hard working lady,” and similarly complimented fellow former councillor Roger Caranci, who left office in 2010 and is now seeking the Ward 1 council seat.

One of nine candidates vying for the Ward 4 seat, Orser said his priorities include cracking down on open drug use, establishing an incentive program for homeowners to build accessory dwellings for low-acuity homeless Londoners, and – as his election signs notably suggest – allowing backyard chickens.

“I made mistakes in the past. There’s no doubt about it. Nobody’s perfect. It’s the perfect ones you got to watch out for,” he said.

Brown hadn’t responded to a request for comment Thursday, but has told The Free Press she’d been thinking of running for several months. She is one of three Ward 11 candidates, including incumbent Skylar Franke and Harinder Kumar.

“There are so many issues that need to be addressed, and they have to be addressed efficiently,” she said on Aug. 21. “The homelessness, for example, the open drug use downtown, especially property taxes – how they keep on going up – and the spending and the roads and infrastructure.”

jmoulton@postmedia.com

stories.title: Luxury London mansion listed for record-setting $5.5 million
stories.summary: A London home that sold for a record price of $5.3 million is up for sale again with an asking price of $5.5 million.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
A London home that sold for a local record price of $5.3 million four years ago is back on the market with an asking price of $5.5 million.

The property at 2-756 Riverside Dr., west of Wonderland Road in London’s Oakridge neighbourhood, previously sold at a record price for a publicly listed property in London in 2022.

Shahin Tabeshfard, the Century 21 broker of record for the sale, says the luxury housing market, which he describes as homes over $3 million, is stronger than it has ever been in the London area.

“People are getting more comfortable with this price point,” he said. “If you rewind about 10 years ago, it was very rare to see homes over $3 or $4 million switching hands.”

Tabeshfard said that the previous sale of the Riverside home still holds the record for a publicly listed sale in the city, meaning it would break its own record if sold for its asking price.

The London housing market previously experienced its worst start in five years from January to April, with March being the only month where home sales were higher than one year prior. The market did bounce back in May and June, with a slight increase in home sales compared to the same months in 2025, before dropping again in July.

Tabeshfard says that, for the luxury market, most are sold off the market, with sellers typically valuing confidentiality more than most people. So far this year, the luxury market is stable, with him even selling a $4-million home off the market just two weeks ago.

“The high-end home market in London is more active than the data might show, and this sale would be on par with market value,” he said.

Sitting on more than half an acre next to the Thames River, the Riverside Drive home was custom-built in 2014 and designed by Bradley Skinner of Skinner and Skinner Architects Inc. The home offers 7,664 square feet of total living space, including a heated exterior driveway and soundproof theatre room, among other features.

Tabeshfard says there’s been some aesthetic updating and maintenance since it changed hands back in 2022, but overall, the property has the same components. He confirmed that, since it was built, this will be just the second time it has changed hands.

Back in 2022, the property was originally listed at $5.5 million. Tabeshfard says the asking price is the same this time around, because he hasn’t seen a significant increase in the market but believes the house has not lost any value.

“We’re priced accurately for where the market sees it. Ultimately, the market will dictate the value. $5.5 million, we felt, is a good starting point to market the property for sale,” he said.

The house, Tabeshfard says, is a one-of-a-kind property in the London area, especially being built with concrete, steel and a glass curtain wall.

Tabeshfard says the current owner of the property has been building their dream home over the last few years and is near completion, which is why the home is changing hands again after just four years.

In 2022, the house sold after just three days on the market, but Tabeshfard does expect it to take a little longer this time around.

“(Friday) will be the third day on the market, and we’re not expecting it to sell by then,” he said. “Properties of this value, they don’t typically fly off the shelves. Last time we were lucky, where the buyer was ready to go right away.”

stories.title: Hot Stuff: It's hard turning an airport runway into a concert venue. But it's worth it
stories.summary: London International Airport as a concert venue? For the second straight year, yes. Part 13 of our series on people and things that make summer sizzle here
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Got a suggestion for a Hot Stuff story about a person or thing that makes summer special in Southwestern Ontario? Email US at curiouslondon@postmedia.com or read our entire series so far right here .

A year ago, Rock the Runway turned the London International Airport into something it had never been before – an outdoor concert venue.

More than 25,000 people showed up on opening night of the inaugural two-day festival, the biggest concert in the city’s history.

But how did a commercial airport become the place to bring this massive concert to life?

Scott McFadzean, London International Airport’s chief executive officer, says the idea for a concert was born nearly two years ago. McFadzean says the airport is always looking into giving the community other reasons to come out, like Airshow London, beyond just getting on a commercial flight.

The idea for a music festival came about as a fix to a problem: London not having a large enough venue space to attract some major bands, though Rock the Park in Harris Park and Canada Life Place do attract some big-name performers.

“I kind of looked at the vast amount of open space we have here at the airport, and thought there could be potential to really take London’s music scene to the next level,” McFadzean said.

McFadzean soon reached out to Brad Jones, president of Jones Entertainment Group, and invited him to take a look at the grounds. He says the Jones family’s history with hosting Rock the Park seemed like a natural fit and the first place to start.

Jones says that when he first saw the airport grounds, he immediately could picture what the London airport was pitching to him. “We literally walked out on that runway, and I just sort of saw the vision,” Jones said.

But to make it come together, they needed the right act.

Hot Stuff: Adrenaline rushes on two wheels at Grand Bend racetrack

Hot Stuff: All you ever wanted to know (and more) about corn mazes

Jones says he gets calls every year from musicians’ agents asking if there are things he’s working on that are bigger in scale to host them. It just so happened that Noah Kahan’s agent mentioned he was playing in Louisville, Kentucky, in early September 2025 and wasn’t going to be making a trip to Toronto.

“When Noah Kahan was brought to US, one of the biggest stars in the world, we thought the runway was the right place,” Jones said.

But to host a concert on airport grounds is easier said than done.

McFadzean says the most important thing leading up to the concert was prioritizing aviation safety, because the airport would continue to operate on other runways while the concert was held.

He says the airport had to work closely with Transport Canada and NAV Canada throughout the process, not only to get the proper approvals, but to ensure they could keep surfaces for the airport active.

“We worked very closely with all the authorities and regulators, including both federal and municipal,” McFadzean said. “It was a great collaboration between everyone, including London police, EMS and fire. A great way to bring US together and prepare for various scenarios that can result from large crowds being in one location.”

The first edition of Rock the Runway drew 25,000 people for the first night to see Noah Kahan – which Jones says is the largest concert in Southwestern Ontario ever. About 10,000 showed up the second night to see American DJ Marshmello.

McFadzean believes that Rock the Runway is likely the first-ever concert to be held on active commercial airport grounds in the country.

Jones credits the timing of the festival with much of the success. He says hosting it in mid-September prevented them from competing with themselves and Rock the Park, and it has the advantage of London’s post-secondary students returning.

“You’ve got 40,000 or so students that attended Fanshawe and Western, and not a lot of them are in London in July,” he said. “You’ve got a whole new audience that’s coming back to London. So to capture that, that’s a big part of why we picked mid-September.”

The first year wasn’t without its lessons, however, with traffic and parking problems occurring throughout the festival and the need to bring in their own power to run the concert, Jones says.

The organization is capping attendance at 15,000 people for this year’s concert set for Sept. 17 and 18, a 40 per cent drop from last year’s record crowd. Limp Bizkit is the main headliner on a bill that also features Cypress Hill.

“We just want to get it perfect this year, so we’ve scaled it back,” Jones said. “Once we get everything perfect, then we will look at scaling it back up for future years.”

Jones says he doesn’t want to make any commitments that the festival will be around as long as Rock the Park, which has lasted more than two decades, but he does see it going for a number of years at this point.

“We certainly have an interest to continue to make the experience better every year,” he said.

stories.title: Sunny, comfortable conditions expected Friday
stories.summary: Friday is expected to bring comfortable conditions across the region, with sunshine returning after some early morning fog.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Friday is expected to bring comfortable conditions across the southern Ontario region, with sunshine returning after some early morning fog. CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison says the fog should clear quickly, making way for a beautiful afternoon.

Temperatures are expected to reach 23 C, with a dry air mass keeping humidity levels low. Saturday will bring plenty of sunshine, with temperatures climbing to 26 C. Humidity will begin to return Sunday night, with a chance of light rainfall as conditions become more humid across southern Ontario.

Temperatures are expected to reach 27 C Sunday and 29 C Monday, with a chance of showers. “Now daytime highs next week 28 to 29. It will feel about 10 degrees warmer than that,” said Atchison. A mix of sun and cloud is expected Wednesday, with a high of 28 C, followed by a risk of showers Thursday.

Despite the chance of showers, Atchison says lots of sunshine is expected next week, with hot and humid conditions continuing across the region.

stories.title: It's Groundhog Day at London hospitals as rodents burrow, chew wires underground
stories.summary: It's Groundhog Day at London hospitals as rodents burrow, chew wires underground CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Groundhogs drawn to good soil, plants and safety from predators, experts say
Amid an ongoing fraud investigation and costly infrastructure problems, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has a new – and much furrier – challenge on its hands: groundhogs.

In a memo sent to staff, which was reviewed by CBC News, the centre’s Support Services department said groundhogs have begun burrowing at multiple LHSC locations, such as Victoria Hospital, Children’s Hospital and University Hospital.
“Groundhogs have high potential to injure themselves and damage critical infrastructure at LHSC by burrowing through or chewing on systems like electrical networks,” the email said.
Evidence of groundhogs started popping up within the last two weeks, said LHSC’s director of facilities operations Chris Askew.

“We’ve had similar situations at a couple of our sites. It happens,” Askew said. “We have large sites so nature does tend to find locations of where they want to create their homes and sometimes it’s around our sites.”
Askew said his main concern with groundhogs on the property is the risk of them interacting with the plumbing and electrical systems that run underneath the LHSC grounds.
“If they were to come in contact or connect with them, that can have an impact on our operations. We want to make sure that doesn’t happen, and we also want to keep them safe at the same time.”
It’s not unusual for a groundhog to chew through a wire, according to Jared John Pineda, who works with Forest City Wildlife Removal.
“They chew through anything in their path,” Pineda said. “They might also confuse an electrical wire for a root because they probably don’t really know what an electrical wire is.”
The hospital is working with an external wildlife removal company to relocate the groundhogs with traps, Askew said.
“We are doing this for the safety of the groundhog as well as everybody else,” he said.
The memo sent to staff specifies Abell Pest Control is relocating the animals. The company was not available for an interview before publication.
While Askew did not specify the exact locations groundhogs were spotted, he said the animals tend to burrow in more isolated areas with less foot and vehicle traffic.

Pineda said he typically encounters groundhogs in large fields on the outskirts of the city or in residential backyards. There, they are often digging underneath homeowners’ porches, decks, sheds and gazebos, he said.
“It gives them a place to hide where they’re not being hunted by predators,” he explained.
Groundhogs are likely attracted to LHSC properties for the same reason, in addition to the soft soil and maintained greenery around the buildings, Pineda said.
“There’s a lot of shrubs and gardens that they have around the hospital. It gives them a nice little place to hang out and eat food,” he said.
Nearby construction at the intersection of Wellington and Commissioners May have also pushed groundhogs further into the Victoria and Children’s hospital grounds, Pineda added.
Both Pineda and Professional Wildlife Removal owner Patrick Blewett said they are receiving more groundhog-related calls in the city.
Blewett said it’s not necessarily that there are more groundhogs, but that the rodents are living differently.

“If the city grows and a lot of farmland around the city is now being developed into houses, the groundhogs aren’t actually going anywhere. They’re starting to live and adapt to the urban environment,” Blewett said. “When they used to just live in tunnels under the ground, a lot of them are now utilizing structures as protective spots.”

Blewett said it’s unlikely that burrowing groundhogs are capable of damaging the structural integrity of large-scale buildings at LHSC, but it is a risk for homeowners with groundhogs in their own backyards.
“If a groundhog is digging and creating tunnel systems, they’re excavating. Anywhere that dirt is displaced, then potentially all the surrounding dirt could start to cave in.”
Blewett and Pineda both advise reaching out to a reputable wildlife removal company if groundhogs are causing damage to property. Otherwise, they recommend enjoying them from afar.
“Just be respectful and observe it. They’re pretty mild creatures,” Blewett said. “They’re not interested in attacking. They’re just interested in doing their thing.”

In a memo sent to staff, which was reviewed by CBC News, the centre’s Support Services department said groundhogs have begun burrowing at multiple LHSC locations, such as Victoria Hospital, Children’s Hospital and University Hospital.

“Groundhogs have high potential to injure themselves and damage critical infrastructure at LHSC by burrowing through or chewing on systems like electrical networks,” the email said.

Evidence of groundhogs started popping up within the last two weeks, said LHSC’s director of facilities operations Chris Askew.

“We’ve had similar situations at a couple of our sites. It happens,” Askew said. “We have large sites so nature does tend to find locations of where they want to create their homes and sometimes it’s around our sites.”

Askew said his main concern with groundhogs on the property is the risk of them interacting with the plumbing and electrical systems that run underneath the LHSC grounds.

“If they were to come in contact or connect with them, that can have an impact on our operations. We want to make sure that doesn’t happen, and we also want to keep them safe at the same time.”

It’s not unusual for a groundhog to chew through a wire, according to Jared John Pineda, who works with Forest City Wildlife Removal.

“They chew through anything in their path,” Pineda said. “They might also confuse an electrical wire for a root because they probably don’t really know what an electrical wire is.”

The hospital is working with an external wildlife removal company to relocate the groundhogs with traps, Askew said.

“We are doing this for the safety of the groundhog as well as everybody else,” he said.

The memo sent to staff specifies Abell Pest Control is relocating the animals. The company was not available for an interview before publication.

While Askew did not specify the exact locations groundhogs were spotted, he said the animals tend to burrow in more isolated areas with less foot and vehicle traffic.

Pineda said he typically encounters groundhogs in large fields on the outskirts of the city or in residential backyards. There, they are often digging underneath homeowners’ porches, decks, sheds and gazebos, he said.

“It gives them a place to hide where they’re not being hunted by predators,” he explained.

Groundhogs are likely attracted to LHSC properties for the same reason, in addition to the soft soil and maintained greenery around the buildings, Pineda said.

“There’s a lot of shrubs and gardens that they have around the hospital. It gives them a nice little place to hang out and eat food,” he said.

Nearby construction at the intersection of Wellington and Commissioners May have also pushed groundhogs further into the Victoria and Children’s hospital grounds, Pineda added.

Both Pineda and Professional Wildlife Removal owner Patrick Blewett said they are receiving more groundhog-related calls in the city.

Blewett said it’s not necessarily that there are more groundhogs, but that the rodents are living differently.

“If the city grows and a lot of farmland around the city is now being developed into houses, the groundhogs aren’t actually going anywhere. They’re starting to live and adapt to the urban environment,” Blewett said. “When they used to just live in tunnels under the ground, a lot of them are now utilizing structures as protective spots.”

Blewett said it’s unlikely that burrowing groundhogs are capable of damaging the structural integrity of large-scale buildings at LHSC, but it is a risk for homeowners with groundhogs in their own backyards.

“If a groundhog is digging and creating tunnel systems, they’re excavating. Anywhere that dirt is displaced, then potentially all the surrounding dirt could start to cave in.”

Blewett and Pineda both advise reaching out to a reputable wildlife removal company if groundhogs are causing damage to property. Otherwise, they recommend enjoying them from afar.

“Just be respectful and observe it. They’re pretty mild creatures,” Blewett said. “They’re not interested in attacking. They’re just interested in doing their thing.”

stories.title: Londoners will be able to file noise complaints online starting next week
stories.summary: Londoners will be able to file noise complaints online starting next week CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
Service London portal replaces existing process using police non-emergency line
The London city councillor representing Old North and student-heavy neighborhoods near Western University is praising an upcoming change to the way residents make noise complaints.
Starting on Sept. 3, Londoners will be able to file noise complaints directly through the city’s online Service London portal, instead of through the London police non-emergency phone line.
The change will benefit both residents and London police, who will no longer have to triage complaints and forward them to city staff, said Sam Trosow, the councillor for Ward 6.
“Sometimes it’s very difficult to get through on the police non-emergency phone, depending on what their current demands are,” Trosow said.

“To have it initiate with the police seemed like a poor use of police resources, and it created a lot of frustration, so I’m very happy about this change because it’s something I’ve been talking to code enforcement and police about for a long time.”
Amanda Pfeffer, London’s director of municipal compliance, said the city had received feedback about the current process, and found the experience could be made “a little more seamless.”
“This way, residents will know that the report has been received immediately, and our noise and parking enforcement officers will be dispatched immediately upon receipt of those noise complaints.”

Trosow says he’s heard from some in his ward that voicemail messages left on the non-emergency line May not be returned, and responses May differ based on who answers the phone. He says some residents have reported being told to contact the city instead.
“I know that’s not what their policy is … but this is just what I’ve been hearing,” he said.

“All in all, I’ve been hearing a very frustrated and unhappy response from people who live in the near-campus neighbourhoods, particularly areas where you’re close to houses that might be considered party houses.”
Noise complaints that May be dangerous, including those that involve weapons, an altercation or a domestic situation, would still see police respond, Pfeffer said.

Londoners can already report other issues through the portal, including road and sidewalk problems, broken traffic lights and streetlights, needles, parking infractions, and lot and yard maintenance violations.
Starting Sept. 3, Pfeffer says Londoners can also use the portal to report noncompliance for nearly all bylaws investigated by municipal law enforcement officers.

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: August 28, 2026
stories.summary: The article Trudeau receives RCMP protection on trips: report (Aug. 21) begs the question does former prime minister Stephen Harper similarly receive RCMP protection when he sojourns in his dubious role heavily funded by the Republican Party as the chair of the International Democracy Union?
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
The article Trudeau receives RCMP protection on trips: report (Aug. 21) begs the question does former prime minister Stephen Harper similarly receive RCMP protection when he sojourns in his dubious role heavily funded by the Republican Party as the chair of the International Democracy Union?

For example when Harper appeared at a Mar-a-Lago gala in 2018? Or when Harper travelled to Budapest in 2023 seeking closer ties with the authoritarian autocratic Viktor Orban?

Michael Luce, London

We are witnessing the decline of the competitive spirit of America.

The demolishing of the standard of truth was the first indication of the American fear of losing competitiveness. Destruction and bullying came next.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is here to build a better country with positive values. Anyone with any sense at all will follow him.

Graeme MacLean, St. Thomas

When buyers in Ontario drive their new $50,000 EV into the garage of their new $1.5 million home, taxpayers, many of whom are working several jobs to make ends meet, must contribute to the $135,000 rebate to which these affluent buyers are entitled.

Bill Caldwell, London

stories.title: Missing Person - Cole Rioux
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (August 28th, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 19-year-old Cole Rioux of London.

He is described as male, Caucasian, approximately 5’8”, 155lbs, slim build, with green eyes, light brown buzz cut hair. He was last seen wearing a black T-shirt, with pink or green shorts, and operating a black Volkswagen Jetta.

He was reported missing yesterday and was last seen yesterday at approximately 3:40 a.m., in the area of High Street and Moore Road.

Police and family are concerned for his welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Resale housing market, already sluggish, could take hit from Trump tariffs
stories.summary: "If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while . . . that can certainly slow things down."
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Ontario’s sluggish resale housing market could face some headwinds from renewed trade tensions between Canada and the U.S., but the impact is unlikely to completely derail its ongoing recovery – at least in the short term, industry watchers say.

Uncertainty and low consumer confidence resulting from the trade war, which entered a new chapter after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, have been some of the driving factors behind slower-than-expected home sales in the province in 2026.

Last month, for example, 16,276 homes were sold in Ontario, a 1.3 per cent decline from July 2025, while year-to-date sales also remain below 2025 levels, according to the latest figures from the Canadian Real Estate Association (Crea).

However, ON a month-to-month basis, July also marked the fourth straight month of gains in home resale activity at the national level, with upticks also seen in recent months in provincial markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London and Ottawa.

“This latest round of the trade war with the U.S. puts at risk the confidence gains we’ve seen in recent months,” said Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada.

“It certainly raises the risk of being derailed once again. But still, our base case is that the recovery will remain on track. It’s going to be gradual. It’s going to be uneven, and it’s probably going to be bumpy but, overall, it’s still likely to be sustained going forward.”

After talks collapsed last Friday, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian products on Aug. 22, with Ottawa announcing on Tuesday a dollar-for-dollar counter-tariff response, slated to come into effect starting Sept. 8.

Hogue, however, said that while the latest tariffs will hit certain sectors and businesses hard, from a larger perspective, “this is unlikely, in our view, to push Canada’s economy into a recession.”

Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat rattles Southwestern Ontario manufacturers

Why Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat could hurt U.S. automakers too

He said that despite the uncertainty of recent months, the Canadian economy has shown signs of resiliency. Canada’s jobless rate, for example, went down to 6.4 per cent in July, its lowest level over the past year. Interest rates have also remained steady after peaking in 2024.

And while sales have been far from spectacular, Hogue also said there’s a lot of pent-up demand in the market from people who would’ve otherwise already purchased a home.

“So, we’re not quite at the point of saying the housing market is about to fall off again,” he said. “We think there’s a bit of momentum there.”

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Place Centre economic think-tank at the University of Ottawa, said the impact on the housing market will depend on how long the U.S. tariffs remain in place.

“If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while, and we start seeing job layoffs, particularly in the manufacturing sector, that can certainly slow things down,” he said. “But I think, overall, we’ve just had this uncertainty for so long that I think we’ve grown kind of numb to it.”

“The housing market, over the last five to 10 years, has had to adjust to so many big changes, whether it be population growth or COVID-related migration, big swings in interest rates, and I think we’re dealing with the effect of that right now, where a lot of the market is just locked up.”

Kevin Barry, owner and broker at Thrive Realty Group in London, said it’s still too early to gauge whether the latest trade-war developments are having an impact on buyers, given August is traditionally a slow month for sales.

“Whenever anything big like this shifts, changes, or moves, there’s a moment of pause in the market, which I think we are seeing right now,” he said.

“But people are also focused on going back to school, getting back into routine, getting the kids ready for the fall, so we normally see a bit of a lull in the market right now, so it’s tough to measure it against the reality of what’s happening south of the border.”

Barry, however, acknowledged worries about the economy have been an issue for many buyers over the past several months, keeping some on the sidelines of the market.

“The big conversation is need versus want,” he said. “If you need to move, you’re still going to do it. If you want to move, you’re going to pause and maybe be a little bit more considerate, a little bit more deliberate with your decision-making process.”

jjuha@postmedia.com

stories.title: Multilingual volunteers help patients navigate St. Joseph’s Health Care London
stories.summary: St. Joseph’s Health Care London is introducing new tools to help patients and visitors who face language barriers communicate when they arrive at the hospital.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
St. Joseph’s Health Care London is introducing new tools to help patients and visitors who face language barriers communicate when they arrive at the hospital. Multilingual volunteers are now wearing buttons identifying the languages they speak, making it easier for patients to find someone who can communicate with them in their preferred language.

In the first two weeks of the initiative, volunteers have helped more than 25 people communicate in another language. There are currently 14 languages represented, including Arabic, Mandarin, French, and Hindi, with more expected to be added as additional multilingual volunteers join the program.

Monica Naskret-Reyes, a volunteer who speaks Spanish, said seeing someone who speaks their language can provide relief for patients who are already dealing with the stress and uncertainty of being in hospital. “When people come to the hospital, the concern they have about their health, the uncertainty, what is going on and not speaking the language is a lot of pressure,” said Naskret-Reyes.

“But when they see someone speaking their own language it’s like, ‘oh my God’, what a relief. At least I can communicate a little bit with this person.” According to Statistics Canada, more than 20,000 new immigrants moved to the London region between 2016 and 2021.

About 22 per cent of Londoners identify as immigrants. Tracy Drenth, manager of Volunteer Services at St. Joseph’s, said the program reflects the diversity of the community. “Patient population is becoming a lot more diverse much like the community.

So, we have had several patients come into the hospital who have limited English proficiency. So, we want to provide the best customer service as possible as patients enter our buildings,” she said. The initiative also supports people who communicate using sign language.

Melissa Fowler, a sign language volunteer, said she has helped patients communicate where they need to go within the hospital. “I’ve had quite a few people come in that don’t know how to speak to somebody, so I’ve let them know that I know sign language and then able to finger spell to me where they need to go and then can take them there,” said Fowler.

For languages that aren’t represented by an on-site volunteer, trained volunteers can use an iPad equipped with an interpretation service that provides access to an additional 200 languages. The live interpretation service is intended for general information, such as finding a department, getting directions or locating the cafeteria.

It is not intended for clinical information. St. Joseph’s says more languages could be represented at hospital entrances as additional multilingual volunteers join the program.

stories.title: Missing swimmer found dead at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: Missing swimmer found dead at Pinery Provincial Park CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
Beachgoers found the missing 28-year-old's body on Thursday, police said
Provincial Police in Lambton County say they have recovered the body of a missing swimmer who was last seen at a Pinery Provincial Park beach on Wednesday afternoon.

Police say visitors to the beach located the body of the individual on Thursday. They did not share any details of the person's identity, other than specifying the deceased as a 28-year-old from Scarborough.
OPP say the search began when police were called at 1 p.m. on Aug. 26, about the missing swimmer who was last seen at a beach in the park.

Two OPP boats, as well as the underwater search and recovery unit, and OPP aviation services, were helping with the search. Anishnabek Police Service, which operates a detachment at Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, also helped.
It's unclear why it took almost 24 hours for OPP to notify the public about the missing swimmer.

stories.title: ‘Dream come true’: New Muslim community centre opening in London
stories.summary: Fourteen years in the making, Noor Gardens brings worship, education and recreation under one roof in the city’s southwest.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
A 14-year effort to build a new home for London’s Muslim community will culminate Friday with the opening of Noor Gardens in the city’s southwest.

The mosque and community centre at 457 Southdale Rd. W. combines worship, education and recreation under one roof. It features a prayer hall, gymnasium, youth lounge and classrooms for educational and social programs.

“This is truly a dream come true,” said Dr. Nabil Sultan, chair of the Noor Gardens centre committee and a physician with London Health Sciences Centre.

The Muslim Association of Canada bought the 13-acre property near Wonderland and Southdale roads in 2012, Sultan said. The organization placed the total project cost at $14.3 million in a fundraising update last year, up from the $12-million estimate reported when plans were presented to the city in 2017.

Sultan said the project was funded by London’s Muslim community throughout the years from donations ranging from $5 and $10 to much larger amounts.

“There’s probably thousands of individual donations that have been made to this project by the community here in London,” he said.

The centre arrives as existing mosques face growing pressure for space, particularly during Friday prayers and Ramadan. About 35,000 Londoners identified as Muslim in the 2021 census , representing 8.4 per cent of the city’s population.

London’s Muslim roots stretch back generations. Families began raising money for a mosque in the 1950s and bought a house at 151 Oxford St. W. in 1956. After fire destroyed that building in 1961, the current London Muslim Mosque opened in 1964. It is recognized as Ontario’s first mosque and Canada’s second.

Sultan, who has lived in London since 1989, recalled growing up with cramped worship spaces and few of the recreational and educational services Noor Gardens will offer.

Its name means “gardens of light” in Arabic, a theme carried through the large windows, lighting and traditional Islamic architectural details inside the building. The property was once home to Wally World, a water park remembered by many longtime Londoners.

“As the community grew, the needs and the aspirations and what we wanted to achieve started to grow with the numbers of people,” said Dr. Munir El-Kassem, Imam of the Islamic Centre of Southwest Ontario.

El-Kassem, marking his 50th year in London, said Noor Gardens marks the community’s evolution from modest beginnings to a new generation of Muslims in London.

He believes the centre will be a place of reflection, peace and dialogue for people of all backgrounds.

A ribbon-cutting ceremony for the public is scheduled for Friday at 11 a.m., followed by tours of the facility.

Organizers also envision Noor Gardens hosting open houses, interfaith events and conversations intended to connect Muslim and non-Muslim Londoners.

“Our doors are wide open for any visitors to come,” Sultan said.

stories.title: Western welcomes 191 medical students amid family doctor shortage
stories.summary: The incoming class received its white coats ahead of four years of training.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
The incoming class received its white coats ahead of four years of training.

Nearly 200 incoming students received their white coats Thursday at Western University , marking a symbolic step toward becoming doctors in a province facing a growing need for family physicians.

The annual white coat ceremony kicks off four years of academic and clinical training for the 191 students entering the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry this September.

“The white coat represents trust,” said John Yoo, dean of the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry. “That is an enormous privilege and an enormous responsibility. Never take that for granted.”

He told the students the most important part of their education will come when they begin reading patients.

“You will be given a kind of superpower, the ability to ask patients virtually anything. Patients will let you into their lives, often when they are at the most vulnerable,” Yoo said.

“Knowing medicine is about what we do with that knowledge. Sometimes you need to act, sometimes you need to speak, and sometimes you just need to sit down, be quiet and listen.”

Among the class of 2030 is Hallee Knelsen, who studied health sciences at Western and completed a one-year master’s degree in kinesiology.

Knelsen, 23, said she has wanted to become a doctor for as long as she can remember, with a childhood experience involving a family member in hospital helping shape her career path.

“One of my aunts said to me, ‘I could never be a nurse or a doctor, it would be too sad,’” Knelsen said. “I think that stuck with me because I was like, ‘someone’s gotta do it and it should be someone who can feel those feelings with that patient.’”

Growing up in Aylmer, Knelsen said she feels a strong connection to small, rural communities and the challenges they face accessing health care.

Inspired by mom's battle, siblings graduate from Western, eye careers in health care

Whiz kid who started at Western University at 15 graduates at top of class

The Ontario Medical Association says more than 2.5 million Ontarians do not have access to a family physician, with that number expected to almost double in 2026.

“I know in my town, even, people struggle to get family doctors and I think it would be really cool to be able to serve areas like that,” Knelsen said.

The shortage comes as fewer medical students are considering family medicine. An Ontario Medical Association survey in 2025 found only 42 per cent of Ontario medical students surveyed were considering it as a career.

Knelsen said she only began seriously considering family medicine over the past couple of years.

“I think, because it’s such a long and tough application process, we all think we want to shoot for the stars and go for the most competitive thing once we’re actually there,” Knelsen said.

“When you actually think about what you wanna spend your life doing, I love the idea of being able to treat patients over the long term and building that connection with them.”

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as Ontario company shifts away from U.S. suppliers
stories.summary: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as Ontario company shifts away from U.S. suppliers CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
Company says it will replace 70% of U.S. ingredients with Canadian, other suppliers by 2027
An Ontario ice cream company says it will replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and won't increase prices for two years.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is shifting away from American suppliers as the trade dispute between Canada and the United States continues. The family-owned company also says it won't raise prices for its ice cream until March 2028.
It began looking for alternatives to U.S. suppliers in March 2025, when the first round of tariffs from the Trump administration was announced, CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“We made a statement at that time that we weren’t raising prices and we were going to start this journey. And here we are. We have not been sitting idle. We have been working very hard,” Chapman told CBC's _London Morning_ on Thursday.
The company said it's on track to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and components with Canadian or non-U.S. sources by mid-2027.
One of the biggest changes involves sugar cones.
There are no producers of industrial sugar cones in Canada, so the company partnered with Original Foods, a Dunville, Ont.-based company, to bring in a cone oven, Chapman said.
“We are going to be the only company in Canada who has a 100 per cent Canadian cone line."
Original Foods Limited will produce the sugar cones for Chapman's. The manufacturer tapped the ice cream retailer a few months ago when trade talks with Canada and the U.S. intensified.

"It's very rewarding to keep the jobs in Canada. It makes our economy stronger and we're not being dependent outside the country, especially when there's a country that tries to make our economy and our lives more difficult. It's nice to see that we can collaborate and give somewhat of strategic response that’s good for Canada."

The two companies have already signed their agreement and equipment has been purchased in Germany. However, Tremblay said, there have been delays due to Canada's electricity registration requirements and other red tape.

"Sometimes [the requirements] are really unique to Canada and not aligned with European manufacturers, so it causes extra costs and delays and is a perfect example of something that can be reviewed," he said.
Tremblay said he plans to contact other Canadian companies to encourage more local partnerships.
Chapman's is also moving production of wafers used in its ice cream sandwiches to Canada, and is sourcing ingredients such as almonds from Australia and cherries from Chile.
The trade dispute has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically, he said.

“The first round last year of tariffs really opened the eyes of a lot of industry in Canada. Companies that we’ve known for years that would never consider producing certain products, suddenly they were saying, 'You know what, maybe we should look at this.'”
He said some of the changes have also proved to be more affordable than expected.

“It’s crazy what this has done for businesses in this country. Almonds from Australia, are you crazy? How is that possible that we could get an even better price, plus freight, from Australia instead of the United States? So we’re finding a lot of opportunities out there.”
Chapman said some of the changes are long-term commitments, including the five-year contract for Canadian-made cones.
Chapman’s is also working to make its production more efficient to help control costs, he added.
“I am fully confident that we are going to make it to the other side of this."
The company said it will continue to use 100 per cent Canadian dairy in its ice cream.

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream ditching U.S. ingredients as trade war escalates
stories.summary: The Southwestern Ontario company is replacing U.S. ingredients and vowing no price hikes until March 2028.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The Southwestern Ontario company is replacing U.S. ingredients and vowing no price hikes until March 2028.

A Southwestern Ontario ice-cream maker whose products are sold across Canada is ditching U.S. ingredients as the Canada-U.S. trade war escalates.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is replacing American ingredients with Canadian and other non-U.S. alternatives, while pledging not to raise prices until March 2028.

The family-owned company began exploring other suppliers in March 2025 to avoid “future headaches,” CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“In March last year, we released a statement saying we would not raise our prices due to the aggravation from the tariffs, and that’s kind of what started US on this journey,” Chapman said.

By mid- to late 2027, the company expects to have replaced 70 per cent of its American-sourced ingredients with Canadian or other non-U.S. alternatives, he said.

“This is a perfect story of Canadian companies cooperating,” Chapman said. “… No interest in using any American dairy or any American products that we can source other places.”

Chapman’s has signed a five-year deal with Original Foods, near Hamilton, to supply sugar cones, with the switch expected to be completed by the end of the year, Chapman said.

“And we will be the only ice cream company in the country that has 100 per cent Canadian ice cream cones,” he said.

While Chapman’s will continue using 100 per cent Canadian dairy, producing entirely Canadian ice cream is “impossible” because Canada does not produce cocoa, sugar cane and other key ingredients, Chapman said.

But “the reliability of the United States is in question, to say the least,” he added.

“That’s what we want for our business. We want able trading partners that are not emotional, and whenever there’s a dispute, we can just sit down and have an adult conversation and get to the end,” Chapman said.

Why Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat could hurt U.S. automakers too

One small business. $2M in exports to the U.S. And now, $1M in tariff costs

“With the Trump administration interfering in the business world worldwide, it really has changed our view and a lot of other companies’ views on who we should be making long-term deals with.”

New supply deals include almonds from Australia by mid-2027 and cherries from Chile.

“Shockingly, they’re slightly less expensive than the American almonds, even when you factor in the transportation,” Chapman said. “There are some companies out there that really want to deal with Canadians and really want to ship their product here, and when you get to the economies of scale that we have, it just works out.”

Chapman said the company is also working internally to improve systems, cut costs and find suppliers that can provide high-quality products at lower prices.

“It’s a really nice time (for Canadian companies), shockingly, considering the trade war, because we’re finding new partners that we can rely on,” he said. “This is a time to think outside of the box and set US up for success in the future.”

bbaleeiro@postmedia.com

stories.title: Clouds, cooler air move into southwestern Ontario, but fair weather ahead
stories.summary: Mainly cloudy skies are expected today as temperatures rise into the afternoon, despite a cold front moving through the region.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A cold front moving through southwestern Ontario is bringing cooler temperatures and increased cloud cover Thursday, but a stretch of pleasant late-summer weather is on the way. According to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison, the front ushered in cooler air from Lake Huron, leading to mainly cloudy skies with occasional breaks of sunshine across the region.

“We have had a cold front come through the area and that is generating a bit of cloud cover with the cool air coming in off Lake Huron,” Atchison said. Temperatures varied considerably across southwestern Ontario Thursday afternoon, with cooler conditions closer to the lake. Atchison said temperatures near the Bruce Peninsula remained between 16 C and 18 C, while London reached about 23 C and Windsor climbed to 26 C.

A few lingering showers were also possible, particularly north of London. Light rainfall was reported in parts of northern Huron County, while London faced only a slight chance of precipitation through the late afternoon. “The probability through the late afternoon is just a 30 per cent chance,” Atchison said.

Overnight temperatures are expected to fall to about 14 C in London as a weak backdoor cold front moves through the region. Atchison said the system will usher in cooler, drier air ahead of the weekend. “High pressure is forecast to build into southwestern Ontario overnight, clearing skies and setting up what forecasters describe as an extended period of comfortable weather.”

Conditions on Friday are expected to be mainly sunny, with only a few fair-weather clouds and a daytime high near 23 C. The favourable pattern is expected to continue through the weekend, with sunny skies and temperatures around 26 C on Saturday. Sunday is forecast to bring a mix of sun and cloud, with temperatures remaining in the mid-20s.

Atchison said there is a 40 per cent chance of showers Sunday night, although any rainfall is expected to hold off until after sunset. “The next few days are looking good with lots of sunshine in the forecast and some comfortable conditions,” said Atchison. Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Thursday Night: Partly cloudy.

Fog patches dissipating in the morning. High 23. Humidex 26. UV index 7 or high. Friday Night: Clear. Low 10. Saturday: Sunny. High 26. Sunday: A mix of sun and cloud.

High 27. Monday: A mix of sun and cloud with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 29. Tuesday:

stories.title: London hospital tackles language barriers with volunteers, interpretation iPads
stories.summary: The measures offer language support in 14 volunteer-spoken languages and more than 200 through interpretation software.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
The measures offer language support in 14 volunteer-spoken languages and more than 200 through interpretation software.

St. Joseph’s Health Care has introduced two measures to reduce language barriers at the hospital as London’s population becomes more diverse.

In June, St. Joseph’s launched an initiative in which volunteers wear buttons identifying additional languages they speak, said Tracy Drenth, manager of volunteer services. Fourteen languages – including Spanish, French, Arabic and Hindi – are represented, with more expected as additional volunteers join.

Drenth said the initiative grew out of an increase in patients and visitors whose first language is not English.

“We wanted to be able to make our entrances more welcoming and inclusive,” Drenth said.

“We had volunteers already doing similar things without the buttons, but then when we sent out a survey, we recognized that so many of our volunteers speak a second language. So that’s why we started offering and showing people transparency and showing that people do speak a second language and are able to help them.”

The second measure, introduced earlier this month, is the installation of “interpretation iPads” equipped with language interpretation software covering more than 200 languages, Drenth said.

The devices are available at information desks at three St. Joseph’s Hospital entrances and the Parkwood Institute Main Building entrance. They can assist patients and visitors when a volunteer who speaks their language is unavailable.

Volunteers are only permitted to assist patients and visitors with navigation, wayfinding and greetings, not medical interpretation, Drenth said.

The measures come as London’s population becomes increasingly diverse.

Teen undergoes Ontario-first robotic scoliosis surgery at London hospital

Children’s Hospital expands pain-reduction program for needle procedures

Census data indicates more than 56,000 people speak a language other than English or French at home, according to a St. Joseph’s news release. The release also noted more than 20,000 new immigrants moved to the London region between 2016 and 2021, with 22 per cent of Londoners identifying as immigrants.

Patients and visitors have been “extremely receptive” to the measures, Drenth said.

One of the volunteers is Monica Naskret-Reyes, who wears a button that says “Hablo español,” identifying her as a Spanish-speaking volunteer.

Stationed at St. Joseph’s Hospital’s Cheapside entrance on Thursday, Naskret-Reyes said she has already noticed greater comfort among people whose first language is Spanish – the language with the most interactions since the initiative launched.

A seven-year hospital volunteer, Naskret-Reyes said the relief she sees in people she is able to help in Spanish “means a lot to” her.

“It’s been a great impact in our patients,” Naskret-Reyes said. “When they see someone wearing (a button), and they feel like there is no barrier, they feel more confident despite of all their worries (or) their concerns about their health.”

Drenth said there are plans to expand the initiative into more “patient-facing areas” as St. Joseph’s anticipates the program will grow.

“It serves our mission here at the hospital, and the volunteers are fantastic people who just are here to help,” she added.

content_blocks.caption: Tracy Drenth, St. Joseph’s Health Care manager of volunteer services, stands beside an iPad equipped with interpretation software to help patients and visitors whose first language is not English. Photo taken on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (Brian Williams/The London Free Press)

content_blocks.text: St. Joseph’s Health Care has introduced two measures to reduce language barriers at the hospital as London’s population becomes more diverse.

In June, St. Joseph’s launched an initiative in which volunteers wear buttons identifying additional languages they speak, said Tracy Drenth, manager of volunteer services. Fourteen languages – including Spanish, French, Arabic and Hindi – are represented, with more expected as additional volunteers join.
Drenth said the initiative grew out of an increase in patients and visitors whose first language is not English.
“We wanted to be able to make our entrances more welcoming and inclusive,” Drenth said.

“We had volunteers already doing similar things without the buttons, but then when we sent out a survey, we recognized that so many of our volunteers speak a second language. So that’s why we started offering and showing people transparency and showing that people do speak a second language and are able to help them.”
The second measure, introduced earlier this month, is the installation of “interpretation iPads” equipped with language interpretation software covering more than 200 languages, Drenth said.

The devices are available at information desks at three St. Joseph’s Hospital entrances and the Parkwood Institute Main Building entrance. They can assist patients and visitors when a volunteer who speaks their language is unavailable.
Volunteers are only permitted to assist patients and visitors with navigation, wayfinding and greetings, not medical interpretation, Drenth said.
The measures come as London’s population becomes increasingly diverse.

content_blocks.text: Census data indicates more than 56,000 people speak a language other than English or French at home, according to a St. Joseph’s news release. The release also noted more than 20,000 new immigrants moved to the London region between 2016 and 2021, with 22 per cent of Londoners identifying as immigrants.
Patients and visitors have been “extremely receptive” to the measures, Drenth said.
One of the volunteers is Monica Naskret-Reyes, who wears a button that says “Hablo español,” identifying her as a Spanish-speaking volunteer.

Stationed at St. Joseph’s Hospital’s Cheapside entrance on Thursday, Naskret-Reyes said she has already noticed greater comfort among people whose first language is Spanish – the language with the most interactions since the initiative launched.
A seven-year hospital volunteer, Naskret-Reyes said the relief she sees in people she is able to help in Spanish “means a lot to” her.

“It’s been a great impact in our patients,” Naskret-Reyes said. “When they see someone wearing (a button), and they feel like there is no barrier, they feel more confident despite of all their worries (or) their concerns about their health.”
Drenth said there are plans to expand the initiative into more “patient-facing areas” as St. Joseph’s anticipates the program will grow.
“It serves our mission here at the hospital, and the volunteers are fantastic people who just are here to help,” she added.

stories.title: Police seize $32,000 in drugs, arrest six people after multi-month investigation
stories.summary: St. Thomas police say a multi-month drug trafficking investigation has resulted in six arrests, dozens of charges and the seizure of drugs
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
St. Thomas police say a multi-month drug trafficking investigation has resulted in six arrests, dozens of charges and the seizure of fentanyl, cocaine and other controlled substances with an estimated street value exceeding $32,000.

Police announced the conclusion of Project Apex on Thursday, saying it began in March 2026 after investigators identified individuals suspected of trafficking fentanyl and other drugs to people considered at heightened risk of exploitation and drug-related harm.

“Fentanyl continues to pose a serious threat to individual and community safety,” police said in a release. “Its presence creates a significant risk of overdose and death, particularly for people experiencing vulnerability.” Between the launch of the investigation and August 2026, officers arrested six people and laid a combined 64 criminal charges.

Police did not immediately release the identities of those charged. The case remains before the courts.

stories.title: OPP search for missing swimmer at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: OPP search for missing swimmer at Pinery Provincial Park CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
Beachgoers found the missing 28-year-old's body on Thursday, police said
Provincial Police in Lambton County say they have recovered the body of a missing swimmer who was last seen at a Pinery Provincial Park beach on Wednesday afternoon.

Police say visitors to the beach located the body of the individual on Thursday. They did not share any details of the person's identity, other than specifying the deceased as a 28-year-old from Scarborough.
OPP say the search began when police were called at 1 p.m. on Aug. 26, about the missing swimmer who was last seen at a beach in the park.

Two OPP boats, as well as the underwater search and recovery unit, and OPP aviation services, were helping with the search. Anishnabek Police Service, which operates a detachment at Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, also helped.
It's unclear why it took almost 24 hours for OPP to notify the public about the missing swimmer.

stories.title: Damage from electrical fire at new London high-rise triggers city safety order
stories.summary: Damage from electrical fire at new London high-rise triggers city safety order CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 9 hours ago
Power, AC systems impacted at South Street building that opened last year

The City of London has issued a make-safe order at a newly-opened residential high-rise on the former South Street hospital grounds, after a fire last week resulted in damage the city says compromised the “structural integrity and fire separations" of its electrical room.

City officials handed out the order to Toronto-based Medallion Corporation on Monday, giving it until Sept. 24 to submit a report detailing planned repairs at 375 South St., a 588-unit dual-tower complex which opened last year under the name SoHoSQ.

Medallion is required to retain a professional, licensed engineer to review the damage, and submit a report on the condition and the remedial steps that will be taken, according to the order, a copy of which could be seen taped to the building’s entrance.

“Failure to correct this unsafe condition by the time specified in this Order May result in the issuance of a further Order prohibiting the use or occupancy of the building,” and/or legal action and steep fines, the document reads.

Large temporary generators have been powering the building since the fire, which occurred on Aug. 20 in the building’s electrical room. Crews were called to the complex around 3:30 a.m. and arrived to find a large electrical panel fire, according to dispatch audio reviewed by CBC News.

No one from the London Fire Department was available to comment on the initial incident, and a department official said any information would have to come through a formal freedom of information request.
In a statement sent after publication, Medallion Corporation said it was working closely with contractors, engineers and London Hydro to investigate the incident.

"We restored temporary power to the whole building within the same day and are working to restore full power as quickly and as safely as possible," said George Espinola, director of residential property management at Medallion.
In an update to tenants on Tuesday, Medallion said a professional engineer had been onsite to determine next steps and the scope of repairs that May be required.

“We understand that residents have questions about how long temporary power will be required and when all building systems will return to normal. At this stage, we cannot provide timelines until the necessary assessments have been completed and we have reliable information to share,” the update reads.
Damian Cowan, a fire suppression installer who worked on the building, was at the property after the fact and saw the damage first-hand.

“I honestly don’t know how else I would want to describe that, other than it looked like a small-scale bomb went off, as blunt as that is,” he said, noting a large crack could be seen in a cinder block wall.
He believes the longest delay getting the problem resolved will be various agencies needing to come in to determine what caused the incident.
“The sooner that investigation gets its foot past the door, the sooner that they can get everything fixed.”

In his statement, Espinola said Medallion understood how the situation has been disruptive to residents, including noise from the generators, and said, "We are looking at an alternative solution that will eliminate the need for generators."
"We will be communicating updates to residents as soon as we have them," he said.
The generators sit just outside the apartment window of Bri Watson and their partner, who live on the building's second floor, and can be heard with the doors and windows closed.

"It's louder at night, and the windows rattle. We have three cats, they can't sleep at all. Two apartments down from US, they have two young kids. You can hear the generators kick in extra loud at night, and you just hear the crying start."
Watson has lived in the building for one year, and says it all adds to existing problems they’ve experienced with their $2,700 per month unit.
“Mid-June, we just lost air conditioning,” they said. Each unit has individually-controlled heat and air conditioning, according to
the building's website . “It took several weeks for them to arrive at a conclusion of when they constructed the building, they didn’t install several vents correctly.”

“Ours is right in the corner of the building, and the corners of the building are all big glass windows. It’s basically turned into a greenhouse in there. When the AC does work … it does cool it off pretty well.”
The fire knocked out air conditioning to the entire building, according to the email Medallion sent to tenants on Tuesday. Technicians were expected to visit the building on Friday.
Hot water was also impacted, but was restored on Friday along with power, according to other messages from Medallion. Watson says the water temperature has not returned to normal.

Watson estimates the building has also seen more than two dozen unplanned fire alarm activations over the past year, something which affects their partner’s epilepsy. They note work is still active on upper floor units.
A fire alarm activation occurred Tuesday because of the ongoing repairs, and tenants have been told to expect a power interruption on Thursday as the generators are refuelled.
It’s unclear how long it will take for power to return to normal, but Watson says they won’t be there when it does as the two are moving into a larger, cheaper apartment downtown on Sept. 1.

“I am baffled that we’ve been paying that much,” they said of their current unit. “It’s stressful as hell to move, but it’s not worth staying in this building given what we’ve seen over the past year.”

stories.title: Ilderton, Ont. vocal coach helps Rush’s Geddy Lee through ‘Fifty Something’ tour
stories.summary: He has one of the most recognizable voices in Canadian music. But after 11 years away from performing regularly, Geddy Lee, of Rush, had to rediscover that voice.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
He has one of the most recognizable voices in Canadian music. But after 11 years away from performing regularly, Geddy Lee, of Rush, had to rediscover that voice. “I found out, and it was a shock that I was his first vocal coach,” exclaimed Ilderton, Ont. based vocal coach Mitch Seekins.

“He never studied voice before. So, everything that he’s done has been completely natural up to that point, which is incredibly rare.” A vocal coach for more than 35 years, Seekins was contacted in spring 2025 to help Lee prepare for Rush’s Fifty Something Tour.

With Lee now in his 70s, Seekins knew the work would be demanding. “The Rush repertoire in my mind has got to be the most difficult rock gig to sing because it’s so high, and it stays so high, the whole show. He rarely gets a break.

So, does he have that in him anymore? What has the aging process done,” wondered the long-time voice expert. Seekins worked with Lee nearly every day for four months, helping to build his voice to withstand the rigors of touring.

The rock icon proved to be a highly disciplined student,” said Seekins. “And he started to see the progress starting to happen, and things were coming back. And it was a lot of work. But thank goodness he’s focused, very focused,” he explained.

While Geddy Lee is his most notable, a who’s who of great talents can be found among Seekins’ roster of students, including Luke Bentham of Canadian rock band, The Dirty Nil. “My imagination is kind of pushed to its limits kind of imagining what the rebuilding process would be like after taking such a sustained break as Geddy has.

And it makes it all the more impressive when I watch the footage of them playing this tour that they’re on,” Bentham said. Seekins has also taken on Rush guitarist Alex Lifeson as a student. Lifeson’s vocal role in Rush performances has historically been relatively minimal, but he wanted to expand his involvement for the current tour.

stories.title: 6 people charged with 64 offences in St. Thomas fentanyl investigation
stories.summary: 6 people charged with 64 offences in St. Thomas fentanyl investigation CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 3:01 PM | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
Police say drugs seized during Project Apex had an estimated street value of $32,185

The St. Thomas Police Service (Stps) says six people have been charged with a total of 64 criminal offences following a months-long investigation into the alleged trafficking of fentanyl and other controlled substances.

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as it shifts away from U.S. suppliers
stories.summary: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as it shifts away from U.S. suppliers CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
Company says it will replace 70% of U.S. ingredients with Canadian, other suppliers by 2027
An Ontario ice cream company says it will replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and won't increase prices for two years.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is shifting away from American suppliers as the trade dispute between Canada and the United States continues. The family-owned company also says it won't raise prices for its ice cream until March 2028.
It began looking for alternatives to U.S. suppliers in March 2025, when the first round of tariffs from the Trump administration was announced, CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“We made a statement at that time that we weren’t raising prices and we were going to start this journey. And here we are. We have not been sitting idle. We have been working very hard,” Chapman told CBC's _London Morning_ on Thursday.
The company said it's on track to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and components with Canadian or non-U.S. sources by mid-2027.
One of the biggest changes involves sugar cones.
There are no producers of industrial sugar cones in Canada, so the company partnered with Original Foods, a Dunville, Ont.-based company, to bring in a cone oven, Chapman said.
“We are going to be the only company in Canada who has a 100 per cent Canadian cone line."
Original Foods Limited will produce the sugar cones for Chapman's. The manufacturer tapped the ice cream retailer a few months ago when trade talks with Canada and the U.S. intensified.

"We knew there will be opportunities for customers who are currently buying in the U.S. to look for local manufacturing and we approached Chapman's to discuss if they would be interested to buy locally," said president Steeve Tremblay.

"It's very rewarding to keep the jobs in Canada. It makes our economy stronger and we're not being dependent outside the country, especially when there's a country that tries to make our economy and our lives more difficult. It's nice to see that we can collaborate and give somewhat of strategic response that’s good for Canada."

The two companies have already signed their agreement and equipment has been purchased in Germany. However, Tremblay said, there have been delays due to Canada's electricity registration requirements and other red tape.

"Sometimes [the requirements] are really unique to Canada and not aligned with European manufacturers, so it causes extra costs and delays and is a perfect example of something that can be reviewed," he said.
Tremblay said he plans to contact other Canadian companies to encourage more local partnerships.
Chapman's is also moving production of wafers used in its ice cream sandwiches to Canada, and is sourcing ingredients such as almonds from Australia and cherries from Chile.
The trade dispute has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically, he said.

“The first round last year of tariffs really opened the eyes of a lot of industry in Canada. Companies that we’ve known for years that would never consider producing certain products, suddenly they were saying, 'You know what, maybe we should look at this.'”
He said some of the changes have also proved to be more affordable than expected.

“It’s crazy what this has done for businesses in this country. Almonds from Australia, are you crazy? How is that possible that we could get an even better price, plus freight, from Australia instead of the United States? So we’re finding a lot of opportunities out there.”
Chapman said some of the changes are long-term commitments, including the five-year contract for Canadian-made cones.
Chapman’s is also working to make its production more efficient to help control costs, he added.
“I am fully confident that we are going to make it to the other side of this."
The company said it will continue to use 100 per cent Canadian dairy in its ice cream.
