stories.title: Six arrested, 64 charges laid after months-long drug probe: Police
stories.summary: "Fentanyl continues to have devastating consequences for individuals, families and our broader community"
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
St. Thomas police say a months-long investigation into drug trafficking has led to six arrests, 64 criminal charges and more than $30,000 in drugs seized.

With help from the Criminal Intelligence Service Ontario, which a partnership between local law enforcement as well as the provincial and federal government, St. Thomas police on Thursday announced the conclusion of its so-called “Project Apex” investigation.

In a news release, police said the investigation began in March after officers identified individuals “suspected of trafficking fentanyl and other controlled substances to people at heightened risk of drug-related harm” in the community.

“Project Apex demonstrates our commitment to holding accountable those who profit from trafficking dangerous substances and exploiting people who May be particularly vulnerable to drug-related harm,” St. Thomas police Chief Marc Roskamp said in a statement.

“Fentanyl continues to have devastating consequences for individuals, families and our broader community. Addressing this threat requires a balanced approach, focused on enforcement against those who traffic these substances, while supporting collaborative health, social service, housing and recovery pathways for people affected by addiction.”

Between March and August, six people were arrested and collectively charged with 64 offences, police said. No details were shared about who was arrested.

During the investigation, officers conducted search warrants “at several locations in St. Thomas,” and seized an estimated $32,185 worth of drugs, police said. The items seized include:

194.3 grams of fentanyl

54.4 grams of cocaine

22.6 grams of methamphetamine

16.8 grams of crack cocaine

487 prescription tablets, including Oxycodone, dilaudid, morphine and other suspected controlled substances

$4,016.28 in Canadian cash

One conducted energy weapon

One crossbow

Ammunition

Roskamp extended his thanks to Criminal Intelligence Service Ontario “for its important support,” saying such partnerships “strengthen our local collective ability to protect vulnerable community members and enhance public safety.”

stories.title: Juno-winning band to headline Western Fair's packed music lineup
stories.summary: The Western Fair is bringing Juno award-winning band the Strumbellas, longtime band Wide Mouth Mason and a long list of other acts to this year's festival.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The Western Fair is bringing Juno award-winning band the Strumbellas, longtime rockers Wide Mouth Mason and a long list of other acts to this year’s festival.

The fair runs from Sept. 11 to 20, with concerts at the Bud Light Music Gardens every night.

The Strumbellas, whose hits include I’ll Wait, will headline opening night on Friday Sept. 11. The Lindsay folk-rock band will be playing at the fair for the first time this year, said Angela Hawkins, a Western Fair spokesperson.

“I think that’s going to be such a good day,” Hawkins said. “I love the Strumbellas. That was personally the one that I was very excited to announce.”

Opening weekend continues with blues-rock band Wide Mouth Mason, who first started recording hit songs in the late 1990s, ON Saturday, Sept. 12, and London-based band Texas King on Sunday, Sept. 13.

This year’s performances will span rock, blues, pop and country – a mix Hawkins says is key to bringing people out.

“Every year we try to get new concerts that would appeal to a range of concertgoers,” she said. “So it’s something that, hopefully, everybody can find something that they like.”

For country music fans, the fair’s final night will feature Canadian artists Tyler Lorette, Carson Janik and Sully Burrows. Lorette recently was named the 2026 Country Music Association of Ontario breakthrough artist of the year, while Burrows won the same award the year before.

A new addition this year is a Latin music day on Sept. 19, featuring music and cultural performances throughout the day, including the Ana Mexico Latin Power Band and Los Grandes Del Norte. Hawkins says the event is a way to bring in London’s Latin community, especially after seeing the success of Latin street festivals throughout the summer.

“I think it’s just one of those things that the community would love to see, love to try, and we really love to have different cultures represented at the fair,” she said.

All performances are free with general admission to the fair. A single-day ticket costs $15 when bought in advance until Sept. 10, or $20 at the gate.

“I think it’s just one of those things that the community would love to see, love to try, and we really love to have different cultures represented at the fair,” she said.
All performances are free with general admission to the fair. A single-day ticket costs $15 when bought in advance until Sept. 10, or $20 at the gate.

stories.title: Fire destroys golf course clubhouse in Huron County
stories.summary: Fire destroys golf course clubhouse in Huron County CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 11:54 AM | Last Updated: 13 hours ago
The Bluewater Golf Course is closed until further notice
The province's fire marshal is investigating after a golf course clubhouse northwest of London was burnt to the ground Wednesday night.
Just after 8 p.m., crews responded to a structure fire near the intersection of Bluewater Highway and Bayfield Road in Central Huron, according to Ontario Provincial Police (OPP).
Fire crews successfully extinguished the fire, OPP said, but a golf course clubhouse at the location was destroyed.
The Bluewater Golf Course and Campground
posted on its social media Wednesday night that the course is "closed until future notice."

"Thank you to our staff for their hard work and quick response. We would also like to extend our sincere thanks and appreciation to all of the first responders who attended the fire so quickly," the post said.
Nobody was injured in the fire, police said.
Ontario's Office of the Fire Marshall is expected to visit the location and investigate the cause of the fire, OPP said.
Bluewater Highway and Bayfield Road were closed for several hours as crews responded to the fire, but have since reopened.

stories.title: Sunny start to Thursday expected across southern Ontario
stories.summary: Mainly cloudy skies are expected today as temperatures rise into the afternoon, despite a cold front moving through the region.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Mainly cloudy skies are expected today as temperatures rise into the afternoon, despite a cold front moving through the region. CTV meteorologist Julie Atchison says some humidity will linger, with a high of 25 C expected.

North of London and across Midwestern Ontario, temperatures will be cooler as winds shift to the north, bringing increased cloud cover across southern Ontario. Temperatures will be particularly cool near the lakeshore. Those planning a beach day are advised to keep the cooler conditions in mind.

Friday will bring plenty of sunshine with a high of 23 C, followed by another sunny day Saturday with a high of 25 C. Temperatures will begin to climb Sunday, with increasing humidity marking the start of a significant change in conditions heading into early next week.

Atchison says temperatures of 26 to 27 C early next week could feel about 10 degrees warmer because of the humidity. The risk of showers is expected to return by Wednesday. “Summer hanging on across the area,” Atchison said, adding that the heat and humidity are not finished just yet.

stories.title: London's youngest mayoral candidate aims to reach voters through viral videos and social media
stories.summary: London's youngest mayoral candidate aims to reach voters through viral videos and social media CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: Just now
Mustafa Zeboon says his lack of political experience gives him a fresh perspective
Media | London's youngest mayoral candidate is taking a unique approach to campaigning
Open full embed in new tab Loading external pages May require significantly more data usage than loading CBC Lite story pages.
While many of London's mayoral candidates are knocking on doors and planting lawn signs, Mustafa Zeboon is taking a different approach.
The first-time candidate has built much of his campaign around social media, posting short-form videos designed to capture attention before introducing himself and outlining his ideas for the city.

Zeboon is one of 12 certified candidates running for mayor in London's Oct. 26 municipal election and, at 24, appears to be the youngest person in the race. While many candidates are relying on traditional campaign tactics, Zeboon says social media is the primary way he hopes to reach voters.

"I think the time of old people ruling everything and deciding what young people want is over. I'm here to say what young people want," said Zeboon. "I'm here to give a new fresh perspective, because it takes someone young to know what young people want."
Zeboon, who styles his campaign name as "Zebuun," said he decided to run for mayor after spending several years in Japan studying information technology.
When he returned to London, he said he was frustrated by what he viewed as a lack of progress on issues including homelessness and addiction, public transit, road construction and property taxes.
"[It felt like] for years not much has been done here. I have a lot of crazy ideas, but I think I can do it and I can definitely punch above my weight," Zeboon said.
To launch his campaign, Zeboon posted a video he hoped would go viral.
"We were trying to make it as goofy as possible just to see if it goes viral, because I know memes sell, and it worked," he said, adding the clip received more than 500,000 views.
Since then, Zeboon said platforms such as Instagram Reels and TikTok have become the primary way he reaches voters.
"I'm a person that keeps up with the times. I don't rely on conventional means exclusively," he said. "Social media is probably your best place for outreach. Attention is currency."
He said social media also allows him to engage directly with residents through comments and messages, while highlighting local businesses and community organizations.
Many of Zeboon's videos focus on policy proposals.

One promotes light rail transit as a long-term solution to London's transportation challenges. The city abandoned previous plans for light rail in favour of a bus rapid transit system, which remains under construction.
Another video criticizes London's approach to road construction.

"I think we have too much construction starting everywhere, and letting it take years isn't how I would run a city," Zeboon said. "I would like to have a more controlled, one area at a time, all hands on deck and overnight if we need to, approach."
Zeboon did not provide details on how concentrating projects in one area or expanding overnight construction would affect costs, scheduling or traffic management.
Among his other proposals, Zeboon said he would advocate for a city-wide online job board connecting employers with job seekers while screening postings for legitimacy.
Homelessness is the issue Zeboon identifies as his top priority.
"What the city is doing isn't working," he said.

He said he would focus on improving co-ordination among social service agencies, expanding supportive housing and preventing people from becoming homeless. He acknowledged those efforts would require collaboration with community organizations and other levels of government.
Zeboon acknowledged he would bring little political experience to city hall but argued that collaboration would be one of his strengths.

"What I lack in experience as an individual, I make up for by having the qualified people on my team who fill that gap," he said. "Teamwork is essential, especially when you're working in a city. You have to have everyone's opinion, and work with that."
His campaign's emphasis on social media is also a gamble.

The strategy depends heavily on reaching younger voters, who have historically voted at lower rates than older Canadians. In the 2025 federal election, Elections Canada reported turnout among eligible voters aged 18 to 24 was 56 per cent.
Still, Zeboon believes his approach will resonate.
"I'm the hopeful candidate for people my age — in their 20s and their 30s," he said. "This is my demographic, and I know people connect with what I'm saying."

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: August 27, 2026
stories.summary: Regarding Brian Lilley’s column Appeal Court kills ridiculous Toronto bike lane ruling (Aug. 19):
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Regarding Brian Lilley’s column Appeal Court kills ridiculous Toronto bike lane ruling (Aug. 19):

Lilley derides the “Charter rights” argument and ignores the argument that removing bike lanes is a bad idea and represents overreach, yet again, by Premier Doug Ford.

I thought we were past the notion that widening thoroughfares to accommodate more cars would reduce gridlock. On the contrary, it encourages the use of even more cars. And this makes cycling more hazardous and even deadly.

Carol Lewis, London

The article ‘I like it here, I am free’; Encampment set up in Port Elgin parkette (Aug. 19) lauds some very poor behaviour.

John Lowry walked away not only from an unhappy marriage, but left an autistic son to be cared for by others. How dare he have the audacity to say, “I am free?” When did his role as husband and father expire?

Then, Lowry uses the overused rhetoric that he had a bad childhood, his dad took off, blah, blah, blah. I would have hoped from that experience alone Lowry would have been motivated to be a better man and caregiver.

In my opinion, Lowry should not be known as a father; that merit walked out the door with him.

B. McArthur, Dorchester

stories.content:
Beginning Monday, August 31, the City of London will be completing curb and catch basin improvements along the Thames Valley Parkway (TVP) in Springbank Park.

To allow for the work to be completed safely, a section of the TVP will be closed until the end of the day on Friday, September 4. A signed detour will be in place in the area to reroute pedestrians and cyclists around the work zone until the work is complete.

stories.title: White Oak Road and Bradley Avenue intersection to close for Bradley Avenue Extension work
stories.summary: Starting Monday, August 31 (weather permitting), the White Oak Road and Bradley Avenue intersection will be temporarily closed for approximat
stories.content:
Starting Monday, August 31 (weather permitting), the White Oak Road and Bradley Avenue intersection will be temporarily closed for approximately two weeks while crews complete the next stage of watermain and road work.

A signed detour will be in place using Southdale Road, Wellington Road and Exeter Road.

Drivers are advised to expect delays, allow extra time and follow detour signage to reach their destinations.

Crews will install a new watermain across White Oak Road at the intersection, replace the curbs and remove and replace the road surface within the intersection.

A watermain is an underground pipe that carries clean drinking water to homes and businesses.

Work on the project has been underway, with crews completing earlier stages of the watermain installation and other work in the area. This upcoming closure is needed to complete the work across the intersection and finish the road surface.

The Bradley Avenue Extension Project runs from Wharncliffe Road South to Jalna Boulevard. Work began in 2025 and includes building a new four-lane road, widening Bradley Avenue between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard, and adding sidewalks, bike paths, street lighting and landscaping.

The project is expected to be mostly finished by fall 2026, with paving and final cleanup planned for 2027.

Renew link: https://maps.London.CA/renewlondon?id=61753

stories.title: Council nixes homeless shelter guideline about illegal drug possession—leaving status quo or confusion?
stories.summary: London won’t enact a new drug policy for taxpayer-funded emergency homeless shelters meant to clarify and standardize admission rules, but the decision faced sharp criticism for being politically motivated and confusing.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London won’t enact a new drug policy for taxpayer-funded emergency homeless shelters meant to clarify and standardize admission rules, but the decision faced sharp criticism for being politically motivated and confusing.

The 2026 Emergency Shelter Guidelines aim to modernize the 15 year old policy , including a clause that possessing illegal drugs should not automatically prevent someone from entering a shelter However on Tuesday, Council voted 9-6 in support of an amendment by Coun.

Susan Stevenson to “remove any provision that permits illegal substances to be brought into or possessed within emergency shelter locations.” “There’s a strawman argument put out there, oh, who’s going to strip search them to make sure there’s nothing in there?” Stevenson asserted.

“It’s a far cry from saying that, and that (drugs) are allowed.” Stevenson argued that the change doesn’t block admission, it simply leaves the updated guidelines silent on the issue of drug possession inside emergency shelters.

“Now we’re making a decision that’s going to create confusion, and this is not an area where we need to be confused,” countered Coun. David Ferreira. Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis suggested omitting the clause would create the potential for a drug-free shelter in the future for homeless Londoners without active addictions.

“It’s just simply going to be up to the shelter providers,” explained Lewis. “If someone chooses to come forward through the [procurement)]process and offer a space that is [drug] possession free, then that will be their choice.” “I think what this is doing is it’s muddying the waters, and we’re returning to a place of ambiguity,” responded Coun.

Hadleigh McAlister. McAlister then suggested a motivation behind the motion. “I don’t like how it has been used for political posturing purposes,” he told colleagues. “We’re not debating a war on drugs here. This is not a pro and anti-drug vote.” City staff emphasized that denying entry to a shelter because someone has a medical condition, including addiction, would potentially be grounds for a Human Rights complaint.

Initially the change was defeated 7-8, but Lewis immediately notified colleagues that he accidentally voted incorrectly. A second vote flipped the result, removing of the clause regarding illegal drug possession. After the meeting, Mayor Josh Morgan reiterated that the decision lets shelters maintain their current rules, “The [shelter] providers can continue as they would.

They can follow all applicable laws. There’s some legislation in the Human Rights area about addictions being a disability, and you can’t deny service. The onus there would be on the shelters to continue to follow those laws and guidelines.”

stories.title: One dead in two-vehicle collision on Dundas Street
stories.summary: One person has died following a two-vehicle collision that occurred early Wednesday afternoon on Dundas Street, just east of the city limits.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
One person has died following a two-vehicle collision that occurred early Wednesday afternoon on Dundas Street, just east of the city limits. Middlesex Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) responded to the crash at approximately 1:00 p.m. in Thames Centre Township.

The collision involved a sport utility vehicle (SUV) and a commercial straight truck. Both drivers were the sole occupants of their vehicles and were transported to a local hospital. The driver of the SUV sustained life-threatening injuries and was later pronounced deceased.

The driver of the straight truck suffered minor injuries. Following the collision, the commercial truck reportedly travelled off the roadway, damaging several vehicles at a used car lot on the north side of Dundas Street.

Dundas Street will remain closed from Shaw Road to Heritage Road throughout the evening as police conduct their investigation. Fairview Road is also affected. Middlesex OPP are appealing for witnesses and requesting dash camera footage from anyone who was in the area around the time of the crash.

Information can be provided by calling 1-888-310-1122. To remain anonymous, contact 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: London, Ont., airport adds Porter Airlines to roster, with new southbound winter flights
stories.summary: London, Ont., airport adds Porter Airlines to roster, with new southbound winter flights CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 5:42 PM | Last Updated: August 26
New destinations include cities in Florida, Jamaica
The London International Airport is adding a new carrier to its roster this fall.
Toronto-based Porter Airlines is set to fly out of the airport for the first time in its history starting in November, airline officials announced Wednesday.
Starting with four non-stop flights to sunny destinations in the late fall and early winter, the airline also said it is "committed to building a domestic network out of London by summer 2027."
The new flights and their start dates are as follows:

London to Fort Lauderdale, Florida, four times weekly, starting on Nov. 18. * London to Orlando, Florida, three times weekly, starting on Nov. 19. * London to Cancun, Mexico, four times weekly, starting on Dec. 17. * London to Montego Bay, Jamaica, two times weekly, starting on Dec 18.

"We are proud to welcome Porter Airlines to YXU and to celebrate an airline that will reshape connectivity for our region,” said Scott McFadzean, president and CEO, London International Airport, in a news release.
“For years, our region has been underserved when it comes to air service, with residents and businesses often travelling outside the region to access the connectivity they need."
According to Porter, the winter routes will operate on new Embraer E195-E2 aircraft, which feature no middle seats.
Flights on the new routes are now available for booking, they said.
It's unclear as of yet what the future domestic flights out of London will look like, but airline officials said they would connect "locations across Canada with Southwestern Ontario’s largest city."
More details will be introduced at a later date, Porter officials said.
London Mayor Josh Morgan said the commitment from Porter to open routes to other parts of Canada is a big win for London as a regional transportation hub.

"This is huge for the region because we have 2 million people within an hour drive of London that can access this airport and use it as one of their main hubs for accessing other parts of the country and the world," Morgan said.
Morgan also said more — and better — use of the airport is in line with London's priorities and needs as a growing city.

"This is an airport that has tremendous commercial opportunities ahead of it. It's got lots of land that can be built on, it's not landlocked and there's huge, huge potential for it as an economic driver for our city," he added.

stories.title: London's Nepalese community 'heartbroken' following deadly flooding
stories.summary: London's Nepalese community 'heartbroken' following deadly flooding CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 10:42 PM | Last Updated: August 27
24 Canadians among hundreds still missing as 157 confirmed dead in Nepal and Tibet
London's Nepalese community is reeling after Wednesday's catastrophic flooding killed more than 150 people and left hundreds displaced or missing in Nepal and Tibet.
Members of the local diaspora are working to support one another while organizing fundraising efforts to help those affected and checking that family and friends back home are safe.
"When we opened social media and saw videos of the flood, it was heartbreaking for sure," said Suyogya Man Banepali, president of the Nepalese Community of London Ontario.

"I've called so many people there. Even though we're thousands of kilometres away, many of US have family or friends there, so we have a deep connection back home. It's a very devastating feeling right now."

The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, destroying several villages, roads and hydropower projects, according to Nepali officials. Authorities warned residents in several districts to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.
Security footage from the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border showed people running to safety moments before a wall of rock, mud and water swept away buildings and vehicles.
_WATCH | The aftermath of devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet:_
Open full embed in new tab Loading external pages May require significantly more data usage than loading CBC Lite story pages.
Bharat Raj Paudyal, Nepal's ambassador to Canada, told CBC News the affected region is popular with hikers and is also a route frequently used by religious pilgrims.
In London, the Nepalese community is raising money to send to the Nepal government disaster relief fund, which has established official bank accounts for donations to support flood victims.
Banepali estimates more than 300 Nepalese families live in the London area.
Although he doesn't have family in the hardest-hit region, Banepali, who is from the capital, Kathmandu, said the scale of the disaster is becoming clearer by the hour.

"Lots of people are missing, so that affects families everywhere," he said. "There has been severe damage. More than the physical destruction, it's the emotional toll that's overwhelming. We have to do something to help."

Kumar Dahal, a member of the Nepalese London Cricket Club, said he spent many years working near the affected area bordering Tibet when he lived in Nepal. He said he has lots of friends there who he has been trying to contact but has not yet been able to.

"I'm feeling like this happened to my personal home," he said. "It's a very terrible feeling, not only for me but our entire community. We've all been calling each other and sharing our thoughts, it's a very sad moment for the Nepalese diaspora."
Dahal said at this moment, the diaspora is trying to come together for one another and raise awareness for how to help the community back home.
Banepali said the tragedy has brought back memories of the devastating earthquake that struck Nepal in 2015, when thousands of people were killed.
He said he can only imagine the anguish families are experiencing as they search for missing loved ones and wait for news.
"We'll continue to monitor the situation and work together as a community to provide whatever relief we can," he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney described the flooding as "absolutely devastating." In a statement posted to social media, he urged Canadians in the region to register with the Registration of Canadians Abroad (Roca) system and said Canada stands ready to provide support.

stories.title: ‘Driving is a privilege’: Woman faces drunk driver who nearly killed her
stories.summary: The London driver sped through a red light at 148 km/h in a 40 km/h school zone before slamming into her pickup.
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
The London driver pleaded guilty in the impaired-driving crash that left Shona Ivany with multiple fractures and internal injuries.

Mitchell Gauthier-Neville is a single dad with a whole lot of regrets.

His main responsibility is his nine-year-old son. His regrets come from driving drunk near a school at the start of a morning commute.

“I’m not the kind of person who likes to cause harm,” the 31-year-old London man told Ontario Court Justice Jason Miller after pleading guilty Wednesday in a jarring impaired-driving case.

Harm is what he caused at about 7 a.m. on March 24, 2025, when he sped through a red light at 148 km/h in a 40 km/h school zone at McNay and Oxford streets in his Dodge Ram pickup truck while his blood-alcohol level was approaching double the legal limit.

What should have been the start of a routine workday for Shona Ivany , 57, suddenly became a fight for her life. Gauthier-Neville’s truck slammed into the driver’s side of Ivany’s Ford Ranger pickup as she legally entered the intersection on a green light.

The impact, captured on video near Blessed Sacrament elementary school, was crushing. Ivany’s truck ended up on its side with her trapped inside. It took London firefighters 40 minutes to extricate her. She was hospitalized for weeks with multiple fractures and internal injuries – and 17 months later, she is still recovering.

“My sentence is not over,” she said during her victim impact statement. “I will live with the impact of what he caused that morning for the rest of my life.”

At the hearing, Miller learned Gauthier-Neville failed a roadside breathalyzer test while Ivany was being pulled from her vehicle.

When he was given two formal breath tests at London police headquarters about two hours later, Gauthier-Neville had blood-alcohol readings of 150 milligrams and then 140 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millilitres of blood, far exceeding the legal limit of 80 milligrams.

SEE IT: Stunning video captures huge crash outside London school

Despite the troubling facts, Gauthier-Neville and his defence lawyer, Nick Cake, asked Miller to take an exceptional step in an impaired-driving case and consider keeping him out of jail by imposing the maximum conditional sentence, otherwise known as house arrest, for the sake of his son.

Cake told Miller that Gauthier-Neville is raising his son on his own and the boy has not seen his mother since before the pandemic. He argued there would be serious collateral consequences if Gauthier-Neville were jailed because the boy would be forced to move to Kirkland Lake to live with family he does not know well. Some relatives had made the long drive to London to be in the courtroom and watched from the public gallery.

“Replacing his life as he knows it now to a life where he’s got to live nine hours away with people he knows as family but doesn’t know well is something I think put a traditional jail sentence outside of the spectrum of proportionate jail sentences,” Cake said during his pitch for a two-year-less-a-day conditional sentence with a GPS monitor and three years of probation, plus a five-year driving prohibition.

He made his argument after Ivany delivered an emotional victim impact statement.

“I think about how close I came to not being here at all, not seeing my children, my grandchildren and the rest of my family and being a part of their lives,” she said.

Ivany told Miller it should have been “a normal Monday morning. I was wearing my seatbelt. I was driving at a normal speed. I was doing everything right and should have been safe.”

She has no memory of the crash but woke up trapped. She lost consciousness more than once and has no memory of being removed from the truck or the trip to hospital.

Ivany suffered fractures in her neck area, lower back and the base of her spine, along with fractures to her pelvis, collarbone, hip sockets, ribs and breastbone. She had bruising and fluid around her lung and heart and a tear to her liver. She needed a blood transfusion because of internal blood loss.

She underwent emergency abdominal surgery that left her with a large scar and is facing more pelvic surgery. She had to use a wheelchair for two months after the crash and needed help with her basic needs. She has chronic pain.

Her treatment and unexpected disruption to her employment forced her to dip into her retirement savings. Money from a GoFundMe fundraiser helped during the first year. She also has lost her sense of security at home and on the road.

Ivany said she needed a cane to attend her son’s graduation. Her recovery made it impossible for her to be with her ailing father in Newfoundland until three days before his death.

“Driving is a privilege, not a right,” she said. “I did not choose what happened to me. I did nothing to cause it. Yet, I am the one who has to live with the consequences every single day.”

Cake acknowledged Gauthier-Neville has a full-time job but also a criminal record from a decade ago. He said he recognized no sentence could fix what happened, but a conditional sentence would go a long way toward rehabilitating Gauthier-Neville.

He said that at the time of the crash, his client had lost his father and a brother to illness, his sister had cancer and his mother had medical issues. Gauthier-Neville was drinking up to 15 beers a day. Since the crash, he has quit drinking alcohol.

Assistant Crown attorney Jeremy Carnegie said a conditional sentence was not appropriate and the case called for a three-year prison sentence and a five-year driving prohibition.

He agreed Gauthier-Neville’s family situation needed to be taken into account, but said being separated from family is one of the consequences of committing a crime.

“As tragic as it is, that a nine-year-old boy loses their father for a period of time, that is the pain of imprisonment and that is intended,” he said.

Gauthier-Neville apologized to Ivany, her family, the City of London, police and the fire department. He said even though he was “going through some things” at the time, he had no excuse for the crash.

“Being a dad is the deterrence,” he said, adding he has no plans to drink again, will seek counselling and keep working.

“I have definitely learned my lesson,” he said.

Miller is expected to sentence Gauthier-Neville on Sept. 11.

stories.title: St. Thomas’ eye-catching red barn wins international design awards
stories.summary: The sculpture’s Gold certification puts it in the running for the competition’s Grand Winner title.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
The sculpture’s Gold certification puts it in the running for the competition’s Grand Winner title.

Drivers heading south from London on Highbury Avenue are greeted by a red barn that seems to break apart before coming back together. Now, the St. Thomas landmark has earned international recognition.

Fading Memories, installed in the roundabout at Highbury Avenue and Ron McNeil Line, received Gold certification in the Art and Photography category at the 19th Grands Prix du Design awards.

Gold-certified projects received an average jury score of between 80 and 100, qualifying them as finalists for the competition’s Grand Winner title.

The Montreal-based Grands Prix du Design competition, created in 2007, recognizes work in fields including architecture, landscape design, art and photography. Its Grand Winners will be announced at two galas scheduled for Oct. 8 and Nov. 19.

St. Thomas Coun. Steve Wookey, council’s representative on the city’s public art committee, called the award “fantastic validation” of the city’s efforts in recent years to encourage arts and culture.

The sculpture reimagines the traditional red barns that once dotted the countryside around St. Thomas and Elgin County. From one direction, it appears solid. As motorists circle it, the familiar shape separates into open cross-sections meant to evoke a barn weathering and fading with time.

“For me, it’s very important that many years from now where it sits, you’ll say, that’s where the country was. That’s what was here, and that’s what’s important,” Wookey said.

The city selected the submission by Shift Landscape Architecture in 2024 from 13 proposals. The sculpture was built by Lafontaine Iron Werks and cost $220,640 before HST, within the project’s $250,000 budget. Wookey said the money came from the roundabout’s construction budget.

“This piece draws attention to barns and hopefully stands as a monument as more are lost through development,” said Mike Barker, landscape architect and principal at Shift Landscape Architecture.

New St. Thomas sculpture puts colourful spin on railway roots

Raccoon portrait lands local photographer in national contest final

Barker divided the barn into sections of varying openness, allowing its appearance to change depending on the direction from which a driver enters the roundabout. The effect draws from his memories of working barns and others left to deteriorate.

“The award highlights the value of art in the public landscape,” Barker told The Free Press. “Many people question the value but it is critical we continue to tell stories of the past, present and future.”

stories.title: SUV driver killed in collision with commercial truck east of London, Ont.
stories.summary: SUV driver killed in collision with commercial truck east of London, Ont. CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 PM | Last Updated: August 26
Crash happened just before 1 p.m. along Dundas Street west of Fairview Road
One person has died, and another person was injured after an SUV and a commercial truck collided Wednesday afternoon in Thames Centre, just outside of London, Ont.
Ontario Provincial Police say the collision happened just before 1 p.m. along Dundas Street just west of Fairview Road, a short drive outside of the London city boundary.
The driver of the SUV was transported to hospital with life-threatening injuries, where they were later pronounced dead, police said in a social media post on X.
The driver of the commercial truck, described as a straight truck, suffered minor injuries.
Dundas Street was closed from Shaw Road to Fairview Road, and Fairview was closed from Dundas to Evelyn Drive as of late Wednesday afternoon.
Police ask anyone with information or dashcam video to contact them or Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Driver dies after two-vehicle crash in Middlesex County: Police
stories.summary: The driver of a straight truck suffered minor injuries, OPP said.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The driver of a straight truck suffered minor injuries, OPP said.

A driver died and another was taken to hospital after a two-vehicle crash in Thames Centre on Wednesday afternoon, police say.

Middlesex OPP responded shortly before 1 p.m. to a crash involving a straight truck and a sport utility vehicle on Dundas Street.

Both drivers were taken to local hospital, OPP said.

The driver of the SUV suffered life-threatening injuries and later died in hospital, police said in a video posted on social media at 3:46 p.m.

Police did not identify the driver who died.

Dundas Street was expected to be closed for “some time” between Shaw and Heritage roads. Fairview Road was also closed from Dundas Street to Avalon, OPP Const. Jeffrey Beaumaster said in the video.

“Please do not go around the barricades,” Beaumaster said. “…Updates will be provided when they are available.”

Police said the roads would remain closed for an undetermined amount of time as the investigation continued.

Anyone who witnessed the collision or has footage is asked to call OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made at 1-800-222-8477.

A Windsor man facing charges related to kidnapping, assault and extortion has surrendered after allegedly evading police since 2024.

Windsor police said Alwassi Al Latif, 29, who was named to their Wanted in Windsor list earlier this year, turned himself in Monday.

In July 2024, Al Latif and another person allegedly abducted a man by forcing him into a vehicle in the 2300 block of Howard Avenue and taking him to another location. Police said the victim was then assaulted, threatened and robbed.

stories.title: FC London escapes relegation with dramatic late-season turnaround
stories.summary: A late coaching change and a group of young call-ups helped FC London earn seven of nine points in its final three matches.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
A late coaching change and a group of young call-ups helped FC London earn seven of nine points in its final three matches.

It was the best rescue in franchise history.

The FC London men’s team used a late-season coaching change and a bunch of green teenagers to vault from the basement and save itself from relegation. The local soccer club went 2-0-1 under interim boss Michael Silvera in its final three matches and will remain in the second tier of the Ontario Premier League in 2027.

“We made the change from (first-year skipper Stiven Mikhail) to our reserve coach and Michael did a phenomenal job,” FC London general manager Dave DeBenedictis said. “He’s been doing the reserve team the last three years. We moved him up and he got seven of nine points for US.

“We had a bunch of under-16s and U17s who got called up because a lot of players were gone and they pulled it off. They were amazing.”

FC London finished with a 5-13-4 record, good for 10th place in the 12-team circuit. Its 19 points were three more than Hamilton United, which will drop to the third division and switch places with Kingston.

London beat Pickering FC 2-1 on Aug. 8, tied Inter Toronto II 2-2 on Aug. 15 and slipped past Whitby FC 2-1 on the road this past weekend. The young squad handed Whitby only its third defeat in 22 games this season.

“That was the toughest of all the games,” DeBenedictis said. “There were six minutes of injury time and they went close to 10, so that was four minutes of my life taken away. It was stressful but we’re still on track. We want to be back in the premier league and, in 2-3 years, we will be in contention to try to win a national championship.”

The club acknowledges it expected to finish higher in the standings and should have won more games, especially early in the season. The optimism is buoyed by organic growth at the academy level and a culture the club hopes will entice players to stay in the program.

London Knights training camp: Blue line a clear strength as OHL season nears

What the London Majors must do to lock up first place: 'We're so close'

“The 2008s (birthdates) just started playing this year (in men’s division) but they needed a year of maturing in dealing with adults,” DeBenedictis said. “We didn’t want to go down (to third tier) because we wanted our 2009s to blend with those ’08s and ’07s and that would be our core for our future. We believe in our academy and the progression we’re seeing.”

Dylan de Melo, the club’s top prospect, started at the senior level two years ago and recently signed with the Canadian Premier League’s Pacific FC. He made his debut at age 17 with the basement-dwelling crew this past weekend.

“He’s the prototypical player we like having in our club,” DeBenedictis said. “High IQ, he thinks the game and finds space. Attitude-wise, he’s a 10 and to play in a CPL game at that age is pretty impressive.”

On the women’s side, Sofia Martins joined Sporting Braga’s U17 roster in Portugal, while FC London grads continue to bolster Northern Super League rosters. Julia Benati and keeper Samantha St. Croix are in Halifax, Lauren Rowe and Kaila Novak play for AFC Toronto, Sadie Waite is in Ottawa and Claire Monyard suits up for Montreal.

Earlier this summer, Charlotte Cromack moved from Wexford to Polish side GKS Gornik Leczna for the upcoming European campaign. Her father, Will, just coached the FC London women to an 8-8-2 record and fifth place in the OPL premier division.

The club plans to wait until the academy season winds down before announcing coaching staffs for the men’s and women’s teams ahead of next year. The U17 girls recently fell to Burlington in the 96th minute of the Ontario Player Development League Cup final and will now push for playoff seeding into the fall.

There are four FC London youth teams, including three boys squads, expected to earn post-season spots in the province’s top minor circuit. That alone is reason to hope another late-season rescue won’t be needed anytime soon.

stories.title: St. Thomas faces $167M debt as it builds wastewater plant for growth
stories.summary: The $440-million Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility is considered crucial to supporting industrial and residential expansion.
stories.author: Brian Williams
paragraphs: The $440-million Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility is considered crucial to supporting industrial and residential expansion.

A $440-million wastewater treatment facility under construction in St. Thomas is crucial to unlocking major industrial and residential development in the growing city and surrounding region, even as the city expects to take on about $167 million in debt to help finance it, Mayor Joe Preston says.

Projected to be “substantially” completed by 2030, the Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility is being built in the city’s north end and is the largest project associated with Yarmouth Yards, the roughly 610-hectare (1,500-acre) industrial park where PowerCo’s $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant and synthetic graphite manufacturer Vianode’s facility are under construction, according to a recent report to city council by treasurer Adam Boylan.
Preston called the wastewater treatment project “imperative” to the development of Yarmouth Yards and the city’s continued growth.

“We sat back and wrote a strategic plan that caused US to start building Yarmouth Yards, and then our second strategic plan now is about the growth of St. Thomas,” Preston said. “That includes really unsexy things like the growth of wastewater treatment, or water itself, or more electricity or better roads. So, it’s all in the plan.”

Yarmouth Yards is a “generational” investment by St. Thomas that has created the potential for “significant growth and opportunity,” Boylan’s report stated. Its $1 billion in “associated infrastructure” represents the largest such expenditure in the city’s history, the report added, providing roads, water and wastewater infrastructure needed to support regional residential, commercial and industrial expansion.

But with $833 million anticipated to come from “new and external” sources, St. Thomas does not have sufficient funding on hand to complete the Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility without borrowing, resulting in an estimated $167 million in debt, Boylan’s report said.
The report estimates that debt will cost the city $9.7 million annually to service after 2030.
St. Thomas considers tougher approach to vacant downtown storefronts
Booming Toronto-based burger joint Rudy expands into London, St. Thomas

“Based on staff’s cash flow analysis and revenue forecasting, the City will be unable to fund its annual debt obligation of $9.7 million entirely through development charges and related development revenues and therefore must redirect portions of new industrial revenues from Yarmouth Yards towards annual debt repayment obligations in the interim,” Boylan’s report said.
Preston said there are still several years to explore ways to help pay down the debt, including funding from other levels of government and revenue generated by users.

“Lots of time to continue to work with the federal (and) provincial governments to help US with it,” Preston said. “We needed a much larger wastewater plant so that we had the capacity to grow both industrially and residential, but the users whose wastewater goes through that plant also helps pay for that plant in the long run.”
Preston said attracting large industries that generate substantial revenue could help cushion potential residential tax increases.

“Our treasurer gave US a very detailed report with a lot of risk analysis in it that said this will not have to be on the backs of the residential taxpayers because we’re doing it and planning it right, and we’re doing it over a long period of time,” he said.

The report provides several recommendations aimed at reducing financial risk and improving the city’s ability to respond to future uncertainty, including continued diversification of industrial growth, maintaining an adequate supply of developable land and adopting a new development charges bylaw.

Boylan concludes the financial modelling presented in the report shows St. Thomas is well-positioned to support the financing requirements associated with Yarmouth Yards and the Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility.

“While the outlook remains positive, the scale of the investment and the pace of growth anticipated over the coming decades requires continued monitoring, regular reassessment, and disciplined long-term financial planning,” Boylan’s report said.
Preston said St. Thomas’ investment will help attract “large industry” to the city and create “generational jobs for the future.”
“There’s lots of servicing and cost that come with developing an industrial park like Yarmouth Yards, but boy, is it ever worth the cost and effort,” he said.

stories.title: Man charged after person sprayed in face with animal deterrent: Police
stories.summary: The other person suffered minor injuries, police said.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The other person suffered minor injuries, police said.

A St. Thomas resident is facing several charges after a person was sprayed in the face with animal deterrent spray during a brawl on Tuesday afternoon.

Officers on community patrol spotted an altercation between two people near Talbot and William streets. During the altercation, one person pulled out a concealed can of animal deterrent spray and sprayed the other person in the face, police said.

Officers immediately intervened and took the individual into custody, police said.

Through the investigation, police said they learned the accused was bound by a court order prohibiting him from possessing weapons.

A search following the arrest turned up approximately 2.3 grams of suspected methamphetamine.

A 33-year-old St. Thomas man is charged with assault with a weapon, assault causing bodily harm, carrying a concealed weapon, possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, disobeying a court order and possession of a Schedule I substance – methamphetamine.

The man was taken to police headquarters, where he was processed and kept in custody to attend court.

Windsor police are asking for the public’s help to identify an alleged burglar and persistent prowler accused of repeatedly targeting the same west-end home over several days.

Police said the incidents happened between July 26 and 29, typically between 5:30 a.m. and 7 a.m., at a home in the 2300 block of University Avenue West.

The man was allegedly captured on video and seen by bystanders entering the property and the home on multiple occasions.

London police enlist special sniffer dog to find hidden electronic devices

London man charged after elderly woman stabbed in home break-in

On one occasion, investigators said the man forced his way through a door before the homeowner found him standing in the foyer. Police said he fled after being discovered.

Police said the man is white and about 40 to 50 years old. He has short ginger and grey hair and a mostly grey beard.

Windsor police released two photos of the man wearing a backpack. In one, he is pushing a dark-coloured bicycle. In the other, he is riding a red bike.

Anyone with information that could help identify the suspect is asked to contact the Windsor police’s Target Base Unit at 519-255-6700 ext. 4350. Anonymous tips can be made to Windsor & Essex County Crime Stoppers at 519-258-8477 (Tips) or catchcrooks.com .

stories.title: Scattered thunderstorms expected across southwestern Ontario tonight before cooler, drier weather arrives
stories.summary: Expect warm, humid conditions today before a cold front moves through the region tonight, bringing the risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Expect warm, humid conditions today before a cold front moves through the region tonight, bringing the risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison. Temperatures are expected to climb into the upper 20s this afternoon, with increasing humidity making it feel more like the low 30s.

“We’re starting to see the cloud cover build in advance of a cold front that will be pushing into the area late tonight,” Atchison said. “You can see the rain developing out over Lake Huron, so we’ll bring in the risk for scattered thunderstorms this afternoon through the Bruce Peninsula, with the rest of the region seeing that risk through the evening.” Atchison said the atmosphere will become increasingly unstable as the cold front approaches, creating conditions favourable for showers and thunderstorms overnight.

“Scattered showers and thunderstorms will develop tonight,” she said, noting London could see storms move through around 10 p.m., with activity also expected in Huron and Perth counties, as well as parts of Sarnia and Chatham-Kent.

The frontal system is expected to move eastward overnight, bringing a shift in wind direction and slightly cooler conditions for Thursday. “That front will push through the area and the winds will come in out of the northwest as we head into tomorrow,” Atchison said.

Despite the change in weather, temperatures will remain mild overnight, with lows settling in the upper teens. For Thursday, northwesterly winds off Lake Huron are expected to generate some lingering cloud cover, although sunny breaks are anticipated throughout the day.

“We will see a bit of cloud cover hanging on, but some peaks of sunshine and not a bad Thursday setting up with the forecast high at 26 degrees,” Atchison said. The outlook improves further heading into the weekend. Friday is expected to be mainly sunny with a high of 23 C and lower humidity, while Saturday is shaping up to be sunny and dry.

“A beautiful day and a great weekend is setting up,” Atchison said. Cloud cover is forecast to increase again on Sunday, accompanied by rising humidity. Temperatures are expected to remain in the mid-to-upper 20s, but humidex values could make it feel closer to the low 30s.

stories.title: London airport unveils new direct flights to sunny spots in Florida, Mexico, Jamaica
stories.summary: London International Airport officials on Wednesday announced the addition of four new non-stop, seasonal flights to warm-weather destinations starting this fall.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
London International Airport officials on Wednesday announced the addition of four new non-stop, seasonal flights to warm-weather destinations starting this fall.

Porter Airlines will be flying direct to the following spots from London’s airport:

Four weekly flights to Fort Lauderdale

Three weekly flights to Orlando

Four weekly flights to Cancun, Mexico

Two weekly flights to Montego Bay, Jamaica

The Florida flights will start in November, the Cancun and Montego Bay flights starting one month later. Tickets for these flights are available for booking.

The airport already provides seasonal travel to Toronto, Calgary, Winnipeg, Cancun, Punta Cana and Puerto Plata on WestJet, Air Canada and Air Transat flights.

“The fact that Porter Airlines has chosen London speaks volumes about the strength of our market,” said Scott McFadzean, chief executive of London International Airport. “It reflects confidence in our region, confidence in our passengers, and confidence in the future of Southwestern Ontario.”

McFadzean said a partnership with Porter has been in the works since before he became CEO four years ago.

“As long as they’ve been an airline, people from London have been trying to get them here,” McFadzean said.

Porter has also committed to adding additional connections across Canada starting next summer.

No destinations have been announced, but McFadzean said to expect connections to major cities across the country, particularly “major markets that people love to travel to during the summer months.”

Michael Deluce, chief executive of Porter Airlines, attended Wednesday’s announcement at the airport. He sees potential for more growth from London-area travellers.

“We believe that there is a lot more potential out of London. That means we are committed to expanding our service from London with year-round domestic flights next year,” Deluce said.

There are about two million residents within an hour’s drive of the airport, making it an “incredible market,” Deluce said.

“Over the last five to 10 years, it’s been significantly under-served by our competitors and people from London and the surrounding population want to travel in a more convenient way, not driving two hours to the closest airport,” Deluce said.

stories.title: London landlord to city council: I kept my word to tenants amid renovations
stories.summary: An Old South landlord is pushing back against accusations of reneging on commitments to accommodate displaced tenants as city council looks for an explanation for what happened and what recourse it has.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
An Old South landlord is pushing back against accusations of reneging on commitments to accommodate displaced tenants during renovations as city council looks for an explanation for what happened and what recourse it has.

The project at 145 Base Line Rd. W., near the intersection of Wharncliffe Road South and Commissioners Road West, involves five existing triplexes having their basements turned into new units – which spurred fear of so-called “renovictions,” or booting out long-term tenants for renovations before relisting the units at a higher rent.

In a letter to city politicians , Carlos Afanador, the principal of the numbered company behind the project, rejected suggestions he went back on promises to the remaining three tenants – saying they were offered units before later withdrawing their alternate unit acceptance.

“I committed to offering temporary alternative accommodation to affected tenants during the renovation process. Alternative units were subsequently offered. The tenants initially accepted the units and later withdrew their acceptance near the end of the applicable timeline,” Afanador wrote, adding he paid the tenants the required three months’ rent as a result, and the issue remains before the provincial Landlord and Tenant Board.

“I take pride in honouring my word and am concerned that council has been presented with an incomplete account suggesting that I failed to honour commitments made regarding temporary accommodation for tenants.”

Under Ontario law, tenants can be evicted from their units to allow for major repairs or upgrades, but they are entitled to first right of refusal to return once the work is done at the same rent they had been paying. Provincial law also requires tenants to be paid three months’ rent as compensation or be offered another unit acceptable to them.

City staff initially recommended refusing the planning application in 2024 for being too intense for the site, but council did approve it, partly based on the commitment from Afanador that existing tenants could be shuffled into other open units while work progressed.

The issue was raised by Neighbourhood Legal Services, which represents the remaining tenants at the site. Kristie Pagniello, its executive director, referred to the three months of compensation as a “red herring,” saying the tenants were entitled to the compensation anyway, and the tenants all expressed their desire for an alternate unit but were not offered a habitable one.

“The tenants in the three remaining units will require the temporary accommodations promised by the landlord (where they will be paying the same rent) if they are evicted at the next hearing of this matter. They will need a place to go to, in the same complex, pending the completion of their units,” Pagniello wrote in another letter to politicians.

“We look forward to hearing the outcome of the review of whether the developer has satisfied all applicable conditions and representations made through the planning and site plan approval processes, and what authority the city has to ensure compliance.”

Council voted 13-2 Tuesday to approve ward councillor Skylar Franke’s motion asking city staff for just that: the status of commitments made on temporary accommodation, whether all other commitments made through the planning process are being upheld and what recourse the city has to ensure compliance. Councillors Susan Stevenson and Steve Hillier voted in opposition, all others were in favour.

Stevenson pointed to the city having little legal authority to mandate alternate accommodations through its planning application process, they can only recommend them, saying she was wondering if the endeavour was “worthwhile.”

Franke said she tried reaching out to the developer for documentation mentioned in his letter, and did not hear back before the Tuesday council meeting. She expressed her desire to investigate what recourse the city has in the future for similar situations.

“Some of the information I’d be interested in is if there is any recourse for the city having been given any kind of incomplete or false information that influences project submissions,” she said.

“In the same way we have a list of businesses that we won’t procure from if they violate contracts, is there something similar for developers who do not meet commitments?”

stories.title: Sports briefs: Knights open training camp, Spence defends WBA title, Majors to wear purple
stories.summary: As the weather turned cooler this week, it feels a lot more like hockey season.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
As the weather turned cooler this week, it feels a lot more like hockey season. The London Knights opened training camp Monday with 80 players vying for either a crack at the OHL roster, or to make an impression on ownership for a spot on an affiliate club.

He says his game is like his father’s but “maybe not the fighting part.” Barch says he’s heard several stories from his dad about the city and the fans, and is excited to be in London “I mean, we have so much young talent here,” added Barch, whose rights were acquired from Kitchener in the Sam O’Reilly and Jared Woolley trade last year.

Friday is at Canada Life Place and Saturday they’ll play in Watford, Ont. in a rink with a capacity of 650 people. “I’ve got a lot of friends and family coming, and it was cool to bring the Memorial Cup there, but now to play there it’s even better,” said Evan Van Gorp, a Watford native.

The game is acting as a fundraiser for the renovation of the Alvinston Arena’s floor. Tickets are sold out but they are selling additional tickets to watch the game from the gymnasium hall and there are activities planned outside as well.

“I think we’ve got a meet and greet after for all the kids to come and meet US,” added Van Gorp. “Just to play there again, I haven’t played there since I was like 10 or 11 years old. It’s going to be really cool.” Spence defends WBA title in Richmond, VA Natasha Spence is now riding a four-fight win streak.

The champion – who trains out of Boomerz Boxing Club in London, Ont. – defeated Precious Harris-McCray by a unanimous decision to defend the WBA International Super Welterweight title. “We went in and we did exactly what we said we would do,” said Spence Tuesday after returning to London.

“We want Clarissa Shields,” said Spence. “That’s been the goal ever since I realized that I could hang with these big girls. She’s naturally much bigger than me, but when I realized I could hang with these girls, I was like, okay, she’s the top, that’s what I want.

She’s back at 160 (pounds), I’m at 160 and I’m strong at 160. I’m on an undefeated four-win streak, so why not? She’s complaining that there’s no competition out there for her, but I put on a fight, put on a good show every time.

So, hey, I’m here! I’m here, Clarissa!” London Majors to Shine the Light on women’s abuse It’s a busy week for the London Majors as they try to clinch the pennant in the inaugural season of the Canadian Baseball League. The Majors hold a two-game lead on Welland with four games left in the standings.

London will be at Guelph Wednesday, Thursday in Kitchener, and return home Friday to meet Brantford. The next home game will revive the Purple in the Park game which supports the London Abused Women’s Centre. The Majors will wear purple jerseys and are encouraging fans to also wear purple to raise awareness on the issue of men’s violence against women.

Money raised from jersey auctions and the 50/50 raffle will go to the London Abused Women’s Centre. If London wins all three games, they will lock up first place Friday, but they could do it earlier with victories and a loss by Welland.

Former MLB player makes history History was made Monday at Fergie Jenkins Field in Chatham, Ont. when former Major League Baseball all-star Yasiel Puig hit a pair of home runs. He went deep in the third and ninth inning to tie Sean Reilly for the most homeruns in a season in league history with 21.

The outfielder for the Toronto Maple Leafs of the Canadian Baseball League has taken advantage of the small dimensions at Christie Pits in Toronto, but his power at the age of 35 is still evident. He has five more games to hit one more to stand alone in league history.

stories.title: Pedestrian struck on Southdale in London
stories.summary: Southdale was closed to traffic in both directions for a time while officers combed over the scene.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London Police Service says it continues to investigate a collision in south London Wednesday morning involving a pickup truck and pedestrian. It happened around 9 a.m. at Southdale Road East and Verulam Street. Southdale was closed to traffic in both directions for a time while officers combed over the scene.

A white pickup truck could be seen in the intersection surrounded by several traffic cones. Police told CTV News the pedestrian suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, but could not comment on specific circumstances of how the incident happened.

Police are expected to provide further updates when more information becomes available.

stories.title: Jerome Rancourt ready to lead Western Mustangs as starting QB
stories.summary: When 6-foot-5-inches Western Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt rolls out of the pocket, it’s a nightmare for defensive backs.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
When 6-foot-5-inches Western Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt rolls out of the pocket, it’s a nightmare for defensive backs. “It’s definitely not the corner’s first choice to tackle when he rolls out,” said Dasani McIntosh, Mustangs wide receiver.

The fifth-year quarterback from Quebec City, Que. is the new starter after Evan Hillock graduated. His transition from backup to starter comes at new head coach and quarterback guru Michael Faulds installs new schemes. “We have him as a head coach, but most of the time he’s our quarterback coach,” said Rancourt.

“We spent a lot of time including a couple of days before the camp started, we had a little retreat. All the quarterbacks went over the playbook threw some balls and it’s been very good.” Rancourt has been used in third-down and short-yardage situations over the past four seasons which has resulted in him racking up 25 rushing touchdowns.

His size has made him the perfect player in those scenarios. “I think everyone knows he’s a bruising runner,” said Faulds. “He can throw the ball a mile, but he’s really worked on his accuracy and his touch. I think it’s going to present some challenges for opposing defensive coordinators.

Is he going to take off with his legs? Is he going to drop back and throw it? He always has a stable of running backs behind him, led by the nation’s leading rusher Ethan Dolby last year.” For the receiver group like McIntosh, it opens up the passing game when a quarterback is a dual threat.

“Just more second chance plays,” said McIntosh. “Anytime the play breaks down, we know Jerome’s going to keep it alive. Guys like me with a little bit of speed; we’re definitely going to try to either take the top off or come back to the ball and try to make things happen.” He’s also seen Rancourt develop the mid-range passing game.

“When Jerome throws the ball, you have to be ready,” added McIntosh who had two receiving touchdowns in 2025. “He definitely has a ton of arm strength, but he’s just working on those intermediate throws. He could run the ball.

He could throw the deep ball. Just having a bit more touch is something that he’s added to his game in the summer.” In a season of change, Rancourt is set to take on the leadership role. He’s been grinding all offseason to handle the workload.

“I was also prepping for the CFL combine as a tight end, but I knew there was a possibility of me coming back,” said Rancourt. “Eventually I decided that was going to be the way. So, I was working with the guys a lot in the winter and then came back a couple of weeks earlier in the summer to make sure we were ready before camp.” One more week of work, then Western will open their season against York on Sept.

6. “Now it’s just about getting the boys ready,” said Rancourt.

stories.title: Booming Toronto-based burger joint Rudy expands into London, St. Thomas
stories.summary: "What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that's what we do."
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Rudy, a Toronto-based burger shop that opened in 2016, has been steadily expanding into Southwestern Ontario this year, with a restaurant at London’s White Oaks Mall and another set to open in St. Thomas on Sept. 11 at 985 Talbot St. Luke McCann, owner of the growing chain, spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison on their recipe for success.

Q: For those who might not know you, what is Rudy and how did it start?

A: A buddy of mine and I started it over 10 years ago in Little Italy on College Street in Toronto, and it was a very simple concept. We were both burger fans growing up, and did a lot of travelling trying to figure out what we wanted to do. But the idea was basically just a simple griddle burger. I remember my mom making them in the frying pan when I was a kid, and then the idea was to keep the menu very simple. It’s a scratch kitchen, so everything is made in house.

Q: Where does the name come from?

A: Rudy comes from when my former late business partner and I were kids. You go to a party or something like that, and somebody’s acting a little out of hand or obnoxious or a little full of themselves. We would quietly say that guy’s being a “rudy,” he’s being rude. It’s sort of just an inside joke that we had when were kids.

Q: You’re now expanding into St. Thomas, what made it the next step for you?

A: We went down and we looked around, we spoke to a lot of places, businesses in the area, and they all seemed to be doing really well, and it was a growing area of the province. We found an amazing location on Talbot with great signage, and it’s a standalone. It reminded US of our place on the Queensway in Toronto. So when you find a special location like that, it’s hard to pass up.

Q: You recently expanded into London in January, what made the city the right place for you?

New cafe brings taste of family's Colombia coffee farm to downtown London

Make it 70 years (and counting) for landmark London diner

A: London is a big city outside of Toronto and when you head in that direction you can see it’s growing. You’ve got colleges, universities, and it’s a big population, so we figured it just made sense. I’ve also got some friends that lived down there that would always message and say “Hey, when are you going to open up in London?” It had been on the radar for a while.

Q: Why was the location at White Oaks Mall the right fit?

A: We just sort of liked that area. It’s right off the highway, and I think the mall is under construction right now as well as the road construction. We feel that once all that’s done, it’s going to be booming. You have the Ronaldo soccer Footlab and the Ikea going into the same mall, so it just seemed like a good fit for US.

Q: The St. Thomas location will be your 19th across the province, what do you think is behind the success so far?

A: What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that’s what we do. We’re not as fast as McDonald’s, but we think it’s worth it. I think what really has helped US expand is attracting the right people to come work with US. If you have great people, you can do great things.

Q: Are you planning any further expansions into Southwestern Ontario?

A: This is a far southwest as we have on the books right now, but we’d like to get eventually to Windsor, and maybe Sarnia.

Q: If you could recommend one thing on the menu, what would it be?

A: My go-to is the double cheeseburger, which is called the Rude Dude. I usually get a side of our thin fries that we cook in beef tallow, and that’s another thing we do a little different from most places, although it is becoming more popular again.

stories.summary: Motorcyclist killed in Norfolk Country crash CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 11:39 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Part of 10th Concession Road was closed for several hours but has since reopened
Police are investigating after a motorcyclist died in a crash with a vehicle southeast of London early Tuesday evening.
Just after 5 p.m., emergency crews arrived to 10th Concession Road between Forestry Farm and East Quarter Line roads in Norfolk County, according to Ontario Provincial Police (OPP).
There, officers responded to a serious crash between a motorcycle and sport utility vehicle.
The 34-year-old Norfolk County motorcyclist died at the scene, police said.
The driver and passengers in the vehicle were not injured, OPP added.
Police closed a stretch of 10th Concession Road for several hours, but reopened it overnight.
OPP investigators are asking anyone who witnessed or has video footage of the collision to contact the Norfolk County OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Loss of Strathroy hospital's obstetrics unit forces pregnant moms to travel long distances
stories.summary: Loss of Strathroy hospital's obstetrics unit forces pregnant moms to travel long distances CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:48 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Hospital closed unit in 2024 following low birth volumes, and to refocus on other aspects of women's health
More than two years after Strathroy
closed down its obstetrics unit, some mothers are describing the challenges they've faced travelling out of town to London or St. Thomas to give birth.

For Melbourne, Ont., resident Tamia Chicas, Smgh is only 20 minutes away, but the lack of an obstetrics unit meant she had to travel twice that distance to London several times throughout her pregnancy for her prenatal appointments, ultrasounds and delivery.

"It was stressful," said Chicas, who had her son in 2024. "When you're pregnant and you know you need to go that far, sometimes you wonder to yourself, if there are any complications ... driving that far is really scary."
The hospital announced in March 2024 that it would

transition obstetrical deliveries to its regional partner hospitals, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital, as it re-envisions women's health care. Its last delivery was
Julie McBrien, president and CEO of Middlesex Hospital Alliance, which includes Smgh and Four Counties Health Services, said the decision followed record low births at the hospital.
"In our last year of providing obstetrical services, we did 59 deliveries so when you factor that over a year, that's just a little over one each week and that's challenging," she said.

"I think what it told US when we did our review of the situation was moms were choosing to deliver in London or St. Thomas anyway. Hence why we had lower volumes because we were a low-risk birthing centre."

However, for some new and expectant mothers, the trip away from their home community has been a logistical challenge. Chicas worries this can have a negative impact on women's health care outside of larger urban centres.

Chicas said she had a miscarriage before she got pregnant with her now two-year-old son and that made her worry about any possible complications and how difficult it would be to travel all the way to London for medical attention.

"I was just scared the entire time during my pregnancy. If something went wrong, we would have to go so far out of the way. Even if they had an ambulance or something come out here, it would still be quite the drive going all the way to London," she said.

Veronica Marchuk gave birth to her older daughter at Smgh, which was walking distance from her parents house. However, for her now seven-month old daughter, she had also had to travel to London, which made for a lengthy and tiring experience.

"With the first, I was able to labour on the couch and we basically just went [to Smgh] to deliver her and it was amazing. It was such a good experience because I was able to let my body do what it needed to. But with the second, we had to go into London for an actual induction and I had to do the whole labour in the hospital rather than being in the comfort of my own home," she said.
Transportation is also not readily accessible for many families in rural communities, so driving a long distance for the hospital can be a major inconvenience, added Marchuk.
"It makes it harder with the prices of gas too. A lot of people in Strathroy would have to take the bus, schedule an Uber or find somebody to drive them."

McBrien said Smgh has instead focused its efforts on other aspects of women's health care, such as advancing its breast health program through mammograms, breast ultrasounds, a new MRI service at the hospital, and breast cancer and reconstruction surgeries. These initiatives resulted from community feedback, she added.

"Those are things that now women don't have to travel to London for, they can get that care close to home. So we are focusing on the areas where we feel that we can excel, provide high quality care, that we can do lots of activity and really be an area of excellence in," said McBrien.

However, both Chicas and Marchuk believe that with Strathroy's population rapidly growing, an obstetrics department close to home would benefit the entire community and provide more incentive for young couples and families to live in the municipality.
