stories.title: Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat rattles Southwestern Ontario manufacturers
stories.summary: Industry experts warn the threatened tariffs could devastate Canada’s auto sector while also disrupting U.S. production.
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Industry experts warn the threatened tariffs could devastate Canada’s auto sector while also disrupting U.S. production.

Southwestern Ontario manufacturers reacted with surprise and disbelief Monday to U.S. President Donald Trump’s threat to slap 50-per-cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts, with one calling it “a nuclear option” that could decimate the region’s auto parts industry while also inflicting pain south of the border.

Trump said he planned to impose the new tariffs starting Jan. 1, a move that comes after trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada broke down Friday, resulting in 50-per-cent levies now being applied on about $28-billion worth of Canadian goods, ON top of sector-specific tariffs already applied to autos, steel and aluminum.

“On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Build in the U.S. and there are Zero Tariffs. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with.”

For his part, Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada will retaliate with dollar-for-dollar tariffs of its own beginning Sept. 8.

Industry watchers said Monday the potential new tariffs would be devastating for Ontario’s auto belt, a key economic driver for the province that extends from Guelph, Cambridge and Woodstock in the east to Windsor in the west and includes four auto plants and dozens of parts makers along the Highway 401 corridor.

“That’s like a nuclear bomb kind of effect that would be bad for everyone,” said Ben Whitney, owner of Armo Tool Ltd. in London, a manufacturer of machinery used to make parts for the automotive, defence and food and beverage sectors, among others.

“There is no auto parts industry in Canada with that, but this would be extremely difficult for the entire automotive industry. This is a 50 per cent tariff in a sector that’s making six or seven (per cent) in profit margins, so something’s going to give.”

Flavio Volpe, president of Canada’s Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, echoed that assessment, saying U.S. automakers would also suffer from such a move.

Can defence spending save Ontario's auto-parts sector?

London firms among manufacturers eyeing U.S. investment as tariffs bite

“The ‘importer of record’ pays the tariffs. A threatened U.S. tariff on Canadian auto parts will be paid by U.S. auto assembly,” he wrote on X, formerly Twitter.

“Without those specific parts, auto assembly throughout the U.S. would halt.”

Dave Johnson, general manager at London-based Ursa Manufacturing ULC, said the levies are so high it would take time to determine exactly how they would affect his company, which makes stampings and light assemblies for companies including General Motors Co. and Toyota Boshoku Corp.

“But if that is the case, quite potentially, all automotive in North America would stop moving,” he said.

“Whether it will occur or not is one thing, but it has the potential to bring the entire automotive industry to a halt . . . so let’s hope this is more bluster and bluff because it seems like a total shot in the dark that (Trump) is taking. The automotive companies, I would imagine, will have some sort of response to that.”

Currently, the Canadian auto sector faces a 25 per cent tariff on vehicles exported to the U.S., but that amount can be reduced based on the percentage of U.S. content in a vehicle.

It wasn’t immediately clear Monday whether the U.S. government would continue to apply that exemption to parts produced south of the border.

But even if it did, it would still represent an effective tariff rate of 25 per cent for automakers in Canada, said Greig Mordue, an associate professor at McMaster University’s Booth School of Engineering Practice and Technology.

Mordue, who questioned whether Trump “understands what he’s done,” given how intertwined the auto sector is, didn’t mince words when describing the potential impact of tariffs at that level on Canada’s industry.

“Frankly, an effective rate of 25 percent expedites the demise of the Canadian automotive manufacturing industry,” he said.

Mordue noted the move would put Japanese automakers Honda Motor Co., Ltd. and Toyota Motor Corporation, which so far have absorbed the cost of tariffs, in a difficult position. Unlike Ford Motor Co., General Motors Co. and Stellantis NV, Mordue said neither Honda nor Toyota has idle capacity to shift some production to the U.S.

And while the Japanese companies May have been willing to continue with a wait-and-see approach at current tariff levels, pending the results of the November midterm elections or a new administration in 2029, the potential new tariff levels change the equation, with Mordue pegging the financial hit for both manufacturers at about $10 billion.

“They would look at that and say, ‘We can’t put any new product or commit to new models at that level,’” he said.

“They like building cars in Canada. They’ve made a commitment to Canada, and they think that commitment is a long-term one to Canada . . . but they can’t look at their global operations and say Canada is going to absorb half of their profitability globally.”

jjuha@postmedia.com

With files from the Financial Post’s Gabriel Friedman

stories.title: London man charged after elderly woman stabbed in home break-in
stories.summary: The woman was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police say.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
paragraphs: The woman was taken to hospital with serious injuries, police say.
A London man faces aggravated assault and other charges after a woman was stabbed during a break-in at a south-end home over the weekend.
An elderly woman was woken by a loud noise around 6:10 a.m. Saturday and found a man entering the residence in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East, police said in a Monday release .

UPDATE – LONDON, ON (August 28, 2026 ) – The victim a 73-year-old woman of London, has died in hospital. Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section in collaboration with the Chief Coroner’s Office, continue to investigate.

The death has been deemed a homicide.

As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has additionally been charged with second degree murder.

Investigators are asking anyone with information about the accused, or any interactions with him, to contact police.

The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 31, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

LONDON, Ont. (Aug. 24, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after police were called to a break and enter at a residence in the south end of the city over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 22, 2026, at about 6:10 a.m., an elderly woman was woken by a loud noise and found a man entering the residence in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East. The victim was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911.

Multiple officers responded. As officers attended the residence the accused began throwing broken glass at police. One officer sustained minor injuries. Officers entered the residence, and arrested the suspect.

The victim was transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The suspect was transported to hospital by paramedic services with minor injuries.

The suspect and victim were not known to each other.

As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

Aggravated assault;

Break and enter with intent;

Assault a peace officer with a weapon; and

Obstruct peace officer.

The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 27, 2026, in relation to the charges.

paragraphs: LONDON, ON (August 21, 2026) – A London man is facing a number of charges after police located an unconscious driver in the east end of the city last night.

On Thursday, August 20, 2026, at approximately 8 p.m., an off-duty London police officer observed a vehicle stopped on Florence Street near Kellogg Lane. As the officer approached to check on the driver, the vehicle began moving and struck a nearby fence. As he approached the vehicle, a man was found unconscious behind the wheel. The officer called 9-1-1 and police and paramedic services attended.
The suspect male was arrested without incident.
A search resulted in the seizure of the following items:
254 grams of suspected cocaine, value: $25,400
Rifle and magazine
Small plastic bags
Quantity of Canadian currency
As a result of the investigation, James Beretta, 29, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
Occupy motor vehicle with firearm;
Careless storage of a firearm, weapon, prohibited device;
Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence and registration certificate;
Possession of a prohibited or restricted weapon or prohibited device;
Impaired operation of a conveyance;
Possess loaded or unloaded regulated firearm;
Possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.
The accused is scheduled to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London ON (August 21, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after members of the London Police Service Uniformed Division responded to a report of a suspected impaired driver in the north end of the city last week.

A concerned citizen's call on August 13, 2026, led police to an unconscious male behind the wheel of a vehicle in the area of Arbour Glen Crescent and Kipps Lane. When officers positioned their cruisers to prevent the vehicle from leaving, the suspect awoke and attempted to drive away, striking one of the police cruisers. The suspect male was arrested after resisting officers.

There were no reported injuries.

A search yielded the following:

204 grams of suspected crystal methamphetamine

12 grams of suspected fentanyl

A scale

Small plastic baggies

Speed-measuring warning device

Through further investigation, police determined the suspect was wanted in relation to outstanding warrants, the vehicle had been reported stolen, the licence plates were not authorized for the vehicle, and the suspect had multiple court-imposed driving prohibitions.

As a result of the investigation, Robert Matthew Toms Roth, 42, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

Two counts of possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking;

Impaired operation of a conveyance;

Operation while prohibited;

Possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000;

Resist arrest;

Use plates not authorized for vehicle; and

Drive motor vehicle with speed-measuring warning device.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to re-appear in London court on August 24, 2026.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Road closure on Sunningdale Road West
stories.summary: Sunningdale Road West between Wallingford Avenue and Robbie’s Way will be closed beginning Monday, August 24
stories.content:
Sunningdale Road West between Wallingford Avenue and Robbie’s Way will be closed beginning Monday, August 24. This closure will be in place until Friday, September 4 while crews install a new culvert.

This work is part of the City’s Sunningdale Road Widening project. As this area of the city continues to develop, upgrades are needed to keep up with increasing traffic and to improve infrastructure.

A culvert is a structure that allows water to pass under or around infrastructure, such as a road or railroad. Culverts help prevent flooding, minimize erosion, and maintain roads in good condition longer.

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Through traffic will be detoured around the closure using Wonderland Road North, Fanshawe Park Road West, and Richmond Street. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Local access will be maintained along Sunningdale Road for residents and businesses.

Residents can access the Wallingford Avenue area using Sunningdale Road from the west. Access to Meadowlands Way, Village Walk Boulevard, Robbie’s Way and local businesses will be maintained on Sunningdale Road from the east.

After this culvert is completed, work will then shift to widening Medway Creek bridge along Sunningdale Road beginning this fall. More information will be shared when this construction is confirmed to begin.

The Sunningdale Road Widening project includes reconstructing the roadway between Wonderland Road North and Richmond Street , upgrading underground infrastructure, adding sidewalks, and constructing cycling improvements. Work is beginning this year, and improvements will continue until early 2028.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules.

stories.title: SEEKING PUBLIC ASSISTANCE IN ONGOING LHSC FRAUD INVESTIGATION 24-93680
stories.summary: Police Seek Public Assistance IN Ongoing LHSC Fraud Investigation Dedicated tip line established London, ON (August 20, 2026) – Investigators are asking anyone with information to come forward in an ongoing i…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (August 20, 2026) – Investigators are asking anyone with information to come forward in an ongoing investigation into alleged historical financial practices at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

The investigation, launched by the London Police Service in October 2024 following concerns brought forward by LHSC, is being conducted as a joint investigation with Ontario Provincial Police investigators from the Serious Fraud Office due to its complexity and the specialized resources required.

A dedicated tip line has been established to support the investigation and encourage members of the public to come forward.

“We remain fully committed to this investigation and value the continued partnership with the Ontario Provincial Police and the Serious Fraud Office ,” said Detective Superintendent Sean Travis of the London Police Service Criminal Investigation Division. “Shared expertise and investigative collaboration are essential in advancing this complex file. We also encourage anyone with information to come forward, as even the smallest detail may assist investigators.”

“Information from the public can be critical in complex fraud investigations,” said Detective Superintendent Jennifer Spurrell, Serious Fraud Office, Ontario Provincial Police. “We encourage anyone who may have information to come forward, no matter how minor it may seem. Even small details can play an important role in advancing the investigation.”

Anyone with information related to this investigation is asked to call the dedicated tip line at 1-844-677-9413, the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: MEDICAL CALL RESULTS IN CHARGES 26-82365
stories.summary: Two in custody London, ON (August 19, 2026) — A man and a woman have been charged after members of the London Police Service Uniformed Division responded to a medical call in the east end of the city. On Tu…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (August 19, 2026) — A man and a woman have been charged after members of the London Police Service Uniformed Division responded to a medical call in the east end of the city.

On Tuesday, August 18, 2026, at approximately 12:40 p.m., officers responded to a hotel in the city’s east end in relation to checking the welfare of an occupant.

While inside the hotel room, officers observed a quantity of drugs and Canadian currency.

A man and a woman were arrested, and the following items were seized:

101 grams of suspected fentanyl, value: $8,080

Approximately $2,000 in Canadian currency

The investigation was reassigned to members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section (POIS)

As a result of the investigation, Robert Degrace, 29, and Laurie Elizabeth Young, 37, both of London, have been jointly charged with possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.

Both accused remain in custody. Robert Degrace is scheduled to appear in London court August 21, 2026, in relation to the charge. Laurie Elizabeth Young is scheduled to appear in London court August 24, 2026, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.summary: Stabbing Investigation London man wanted London, ON (August 20, 2026) – A London man is wanted in connection with a stabbing that left another man with life-threatening injuries. On August 16, 2026, shortly before 4 a.m., London police…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (August 20, 2026) – A London man is wanted in connection with a stabbing that left another man with life-threatening injuries.

On August 16, 2026, shortly before 4 a.m., London police responded to a reported stabbing in the 400-block of Dundas Street. Officers located an adult male suffering from injuries, including multiple stab wounds. He was transported to hospital by paramedic services with life-threatening injuries.

The investigation was reassigned to members of the LPS Major Crime Section.

Video surveillance was obtained, and investigators identified a suspect male.

As a result of the investigation, Tyler James Lyttle, 40, of London, has not been located, and as a result, has been charged by way of warrant of arrest in relation to the following offences:

· Aggravated assault, and

· Fail to comply with probation order

A photograph of the suspect is being shared, in the hope that members of the public can assist police in locating him. Members of the public are reminded not to approach the suspect, and to call 9-1-1 if seen.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules.

Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Businesses will remain accessible.

stories.title: City advances key priorities at AMO Conference in Ottawa
stories.summary: A City of London delegation met with provincial ministers and officials during the 2026 Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) Confer
stories.content:
A City of London delegation met with provincial ministers and officials during the 2026 Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) Conference in Ottawa to advance key priorities for London and Southwestern Ontario, focused on strengthening public safety, supporting housing and homelessness services, and advancing regional transportation and economic growth.

London was represented by Mayor Josh Morgan, as well as Councillors Steve Lehman, Corrine Rahman, Susan Stevenson and Anna Hopkins, who was re-elected to the AMO Board of Directors, continuing London’s representation at the provincial municipal table. Council members were accompanied by representatives from London Hydro and Fanshawe College, as well as senior City staff.

“London and cities across Ontario are facing significant challenges that require real province-wide planning and coordinated action if we’re going to turn the corner,” said Mayor Josh Morgan. From homelessness and public safety to transportation and economic growth, none of these issues can be solved by one level of government alone. That’s why AMO is an important opportunity to be at the table with provincial ministers and officials to drive investments, partnerships and policies that can make a difference for residents. We came to Ottawa alongside our municipal colleagues with a clear set of priorities, and we’ll keep pushing to turn these conversations into action for London and Southwestern Ontario.”

Among the key priorities discussed by the City of London and provincial representatives were:

Having the province take over ownership and maintenance of Highbury Avenue and supporting more reliable and frequent passenger rail service through High Performance Rail in Southwestern Ontario. These priorities were discussed with the Ministry of Transportation as part of a joint delegation with the City of St. Thomas and Elgin County.

Additional operating support for Highly Supportive Housing with the Ministry of Health.

Increased support for homelessness prevention with the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing.

Provincial support to advance the new London Emergency Services Campus with the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Support for the Aerospace Innovation Corridor at London International Airport with the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade.

“AMO provides a valuable forum to build relationships and advance projects that respond to some of the most significant pressures facing our community,” said City Manager Sandra Datars Bere. “We appreciated the productive discussions and will continue working with provincial partners on next steps.”

The City will build on these discussions by working with provincial ministries and regional partners to identify next steps and move these priorities toward implementation.

stories.summary: Assault Investigation 26-81156 Assault Investigation London man arrested London, ON (August 18, 2026) – A London man was arrested after an assault in the downtown core over the weekend. On Saturday, August 15, 2026, at approximately 12:50 a.m., a man was standing in line outside…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (August 18, 2026) – A London man was arrested after an assault in the downtown core over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 15, 2026, at approximately 12:50 a.m., a man was standing in line outside an establishment in the area of Richmond and John streets when he was approached by a male.

The victim was assaulted by the suspect male and police were contacted.

Emergency services attended, and the victim was transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.

A description of the suspect male was provided to police. Video surveillance footage was also obtained, and at approximately 1 a.m., officers located and arrested the suspect nearby.

The victim and suspect were not known to each other.

As a result of the investigation, Deionte Lord, 29, of London, has been charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm.

The accused has an upcoming court date of September 16, 2026, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Candidate nomination period closes August 21 for London’s 2026 municipal election
stories.summary: Anyone planning to run for Mayor, City Councillor or School Board Trustee in London’s 2026 municipal election must file their nomination no l
stories.content:
Anyone planning to run for Mayor, City Councillor or School Board Trustee in London’s 2026 municipal election must file their nomination no later than 2 p.m. on Friday, August 21, 2026.

Nominations must be filed in person at the Elections Office, located on the first floor of City Hall, 300 Dufferin Avenue. Electronic submissions are not accepted.

Individuals filing a nomination must provide:

A completed Nomination Form

Signatures from 25 eligible voters supporting the nomination for Mayor and City Councillor candidates

A completed Declaration of Qualifications

Current identification

The required nomination fee of $200 for Mayor or $100 for City Councillor and School Board Trustee

Candidates are also required to swear an oath at the Elections Office.

No later than 2 p.m. on Friday, August 21, is also the deadline for registered candidates to withdraw their nomination. Withdrawals must be submitted in writing and filed in person.

The City Clerk will review and certify nominations following the deadline. The certified list of candidates will be posted at London.CA/elections .

London’s 2026 municipal election will take place on Monday, October 26, 2026, with voting available from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Advance voting will also be available at polling stations across London on:

Thursday, October 1, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Saturday, October 3, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Monday, October 5 through Saturday, October 10, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. each day

For more information about becoming a candidate, voting dates and election requirements, visit London.CA/elections or email elections@London.CA .

stories.title: BREAK AND ENTER 26-81393
stories.summary: Break AND Enter 26-81393 Break AND Enter Investigation Two Londoners facing charges London, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have laid charges following an attempted break and enter involving a firearm over the w…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have laid charges following an attempted break and enter involving a firearm over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 15, 2026, shortly before 7 p.m., members of the London Police Service responded to a residence on Lovett Street after receiving reports of an attempted break-in involving an armed suspect.

Two individuals attended the residence and attempted to break into the home while two adult occupants were inside. During the incident, threats were made toward the occupants and a firearm was pointed at one of the victims. A window of the residence was also damaged during the incident.

The victims contacted 9-1-1 and remained inside the residence while officers responded.

Members of the Uniformed Division and Emergency Response Unit attended the area. Within minutes, officers located and arrested a male suspect on Chesley Avenue. During the arrest, officers recovered an imitation firearm and approximately 500 Nabilone pills.

A second suspect was located a short time later in the backyard of a residence on Dame Street and was arrested without incident.

The accused and victims were known to each other. There were no reported injuries.

As a result of the investigation, Daniel Francis Edward MacDonald, 43, of London, has been charged with:

Break and enter with intent;

Pointing a firearm;

Two counts of possession of a firearm contrary to a prohibition order;

Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm; and

Possession of a Schedule II substance.

Julie Marshall, 23, of London, has been charged with:

Break and enter with intent.

Both accused remain in custody and are scheduled to reappear in London court on August 18, 2026, in relation to the charges.

The London Police Service would like to remind residents that if they witness suspicious, threatening or criminal activity, they should contact police immediately. Timely reporting can play a critical role in protecting public safety and assisting investigations.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Serious Motor Vehicle Collision 26-81112
stories.summary: Update - London, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Road Safety Section continue to investigate a serious motor vehicle collision from over the weekend.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
UPDATE - LONDON, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Road Safety Section continue to investigate a serious motor vehicle collision from over the weekend.

A female passenger of one of the vehicles was transported to hospital by paramedic services with life-threatening injuries and has since succumbed to those injuries.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area on August 14, 2026, between 9:20 and 9:40 p.m. and may have witnessed the collision, or who has dashcam, residential or business surveillance footage, to contact the London Police Service or Crime Stoppers.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

LONDON, ON (August 14, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section are investigating a motor vehicle collision that occurred in the city’s east end late this evening.

On Friday, August 14, 2026, at approximately 9:30 p.m., emergency crews responded to a serious motor vehicle collision on Veterans Memorial Pkwy at Bradley Ave involving multiple motor vehicles.

All vehicles involved remained on scene.

Four individuals involved in the collision were transported to hospital with serious life-threatening injuries.

The intersection is temporarily closed, including Veterans Memorial Pkwy’s exit at highway 401 (From Wilton Grove to Hamilton Road) for accident reconstruction.

The investigation has now been taken over by the LPS Road Safety Section and remains ongoing.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 9:00 p.m. – 9:30 p.m. and may have witnessed the collision, or who have dashcam, residential, or business surveillance footage, to please contact us.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Temporary road closures for culvert replacements on Wellington Road South
stories.summary: The City of London will be undertaking culvert replacements this summer and into the fall which will mean temporary road closures as the work
stories.content:
The City of London will be undertaking culvert replacements this summer and into the fall which will mean temporary road closures as the work gets underway. This work is being done primarily on Wellington Road South.

The culvert replacement program will take place at the following locations and dates:

Wellington Rd South – between Harry White Drive and Fisher Lane - August 17 to August 28

Wellington Road/Glanworth Drive - east/west section of Glanworth Drive to August 17 – August 28

What is a culvert?

A culvert is a structure that allows water to pass under or around infrastructure, such as a road or railroad. Culverts help prevent flooding, minimize erosion, and maintain roads in good condition longer.

Why is this happening now?

Repairs and replacement in the near term are required to ensure structural integrity, address safety hazards, protect infrastructure from damage due to stream water fluctuation and precipitation runoff, prevent upstream flooding, and ensure compliance with environmental standards.

Transportation impacts

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Please follow the detour signage. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Above: A map showing the project areas for the culvert replacements on Wellington Road.

You can learn more on Renew London .

stories.title: TWO STOLEN VEHICLES RECOVERED 26-80132
stories.summary: London, ON (August 14, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have arrested a London man after recovering two stolen vehicles and determining he was operating both while prohibited from driving. On August 2, 2026, an off-duty London police officer observed a man known to police driving a white Dodge Ram displayi…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (August 14, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have arrested a London man after recovering two stolen vehicles and determining he was operating both while prohibited from driving. On August 2, 2026, an off-duty London police officer observed a man known to police driving a white Dodge Ram displaying an Ontario licence plate at a gas station on Hamilton Road. Investigators confirmed the suspect was a prohibited driver, that the licence plate was not registered to the vehicle and believed cloned plates were being used. Police attended the suspect male’s place of work in the south end of the city on August 13, 2026, where they located the Dodge Ram and confirmed it had been previously reported stolen. The suspect was arrested without incident. Investigators determined the suspect had arrived at work operating a 2013 Harley-Davidson motorcycle that had also been reported stolen two days earlier. As a result of the investigation, Richard Kyle Newstead, 45, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

• Two counts of operation of a conveyance while prohibited; • Two counts of possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000; and • Two counts of breach of probation.

The accused has been released from custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on September 9, 2026, in relation to the charges. Investigators believe the accused may have been operating the stolen truck and motorcycle throughout London and area for a significant period of time and are seeking additional information from the public. “We are asking anyone who may have seen the accused operating either of these vehicles, or who has information about the accused’s activities to contact police,” said Detective Inspector Sean Travis, of the Investigative Services Branch of the London Police Service. “Even seemingly minor information could help investigators establish timelines and identify additional locations connected to this investigation.” Anyone who has information related to the accused, the involved vehicles, or this investigation, is asked to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Registration now open for the 2026 Age Friendly London Conference
stories.summary: Registration is now open for the 2026 Age Friendly London Conference, inviting Londoners to connect, learn and discover resource
stories.content:
Registration is now open for the 2026 Age Friendly London Conference, inviting Londoners to connect, learn and discover resources that support healthy aging in London.

Presented by the Age Friendly London Network, this year’s conference takes place on Wednesday, October 14, at the Best Western Lamplighter Inn. The annual event brings together local organizations, health professionals, community leaders and residents for a full day of learning, conversation and connection focused on building a more age-friendly community.

The conference will once again feature, expert speakers, engaging presentations, interactive sessions and an exhibitor marketplace showcasing programs, services and supports available to older adults across London and Middlesex. Headlining this year's program is keynote speaker Mary Lou Smoke, whose presentation, Medicine and Song, will explore the power of culture, storytelling and healing.

"Creating an age-friendly city means ensuring older adults have access to information, resources and opportunities to stay connected to their community," says Cheryl Smith, Deputy City Manager, Neighbourhood and Community-Wide Services. "The Age Friendly London Conference brings people together to learn from one another, discover valuable local services and explore practical ways to support healthy aging."

The conference reflects London's ongoing commitment to fostering an inclusive community where people can age well. Since becoming the first Canadian city to join the World Health Organization's Global Network of Age-friendly Cities in 2010, London has continued to work alongside residents and community partners to improve the quality of life for older adults.

For additional conference details, including the full agenda and registration information, visit London.CA/AFLConference .

About Age Friendly London

The Age Friendly London Network is a collaborative group of older adults, caregivers, service providers and community members working together to make London a more age-friendly city. Through partnerships, education and community action, the Network supports initiatives that help older adults remain active, connected and engaged in all aspects of community life. To learn more, visit London.CA/AgeFriendly .

"Creating an age-friendly city means ensuring older adults have access to information, resources and opportunities to stay connected to their community," says Cheryl Smith, Deputy City Manager, Neighbourhood and Community-Wide Services. "The Age Friendly London Conference brings people together to learn from one another, discover valuable local services and explore practical ways to support healthy aging."

The conference reflects London's ongoing commitment to fostering an inclusive community where people can age well. Since becoming the first Canadian city to join the World Health Organization's Global Network of Age-friendly Cities in 2010, London has continued to work alongside residents and community partners to improve the quality of life for older adults.
For additional conference details, including the full agenda and registration information, visit London.CA/AFLConference .
About Age Friendly London

The Age Friendly London Network is a collaborative group of older adults, caregivers, service providers and community members working together to make London a more age-friendly city. Through partnerships, education and community action, the Network supports initiatives that help older adults remain active, connected and engaged in all aspects of community life. To learn more, visit London.CA/AgeFriendly .

stories.title: London surpasses Housing Accelerator Fund target ahead of federal deadline
stories.summary: The City of London is pleased to announce that it has surpassed its three-year Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) target of 11,803 new housing un
stories.content:
The City of London is pleased to announce that it has surpassed its three-year Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) target of 11,803 new housing units, reaching 11,966 new units four weeks ahead of the September 7, 2026 federal deadline.

The milestone reflects continued housing growth across London and the collective efforts of City Council and staff, builders, developers, non-profit housing providers and other partners to increase housing supply across the city.

“Surpassing our Housing Accelerator Fund target is a significant achievement for London, and it demonstrates what is possible when we set ambitious goals and have the leadership to deliver on them,” says Mayor Josh Morgan. “This progress didn’t happen by accident. It is the result of deliberate choices, a focused approach to getting housing built, and policies that have removed barriers and accelerated approvals. The federal investment through HAF has been an important partner, but it is the decisions we have made here in London that are turning that investment into real homes and real results. As we look ahead, Londoners should know that the work is not finished, and that staying focused on building more housing, creating affordability and keeping our city moving forward will require steady leadership and a willingness to keep delivering.”

The Housing Accelerator Fund is a federal program delivered through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc) that provides funding to municipalities to accelerate housing construction and support lasting changes that increase housing supply.

“This milestone represents an extraordinary amount of work by people across the Corporation and throughout London’s building and development industry,” says Scott Mathers, Deputy City Manager, Housing and Community Growth. “HAF provided London with an important federal investment that allowed US to move more quickly and try new approaches to supporting housing development. Our staff embraced that challenge, and our builders and developers continued to bring projects forward and turn approvals into new homes. Everyone involved should be proud of what we have accomplished together.”

London has also completed all 11 initiatives included in its HAF action Plan. Together, the initiatives have helped increase housing supply by:

enabling higher-density housing near rapid transit routes

supporting office-to-residential conversions that have created new homes downtown

providing incentives for Transit-Oriented Development and Additional Residential Units

expanding financial incentives for homeowners and builders to create new housing

improving development approval processes and reducing barriers to housing construction

investing in infrastructure needed to support housing growth in key areas of the city

supporting new affordable and highly supportive housing through partnerships with housing providers

While London has now surpassed its housing supply growth target, approval of the fourth and final Housing Accelerator Fund payment remains subject to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation’s review of London’s third-year HAF report. That review will include confirmation that the requirements of the funding agreement have been met and an assessment of London’s performance against all targets under the agreement.

Reaching the HAF target is an important milestone in London’s broader efforts to respond to continued growth and housing needs. The City will continue working with the building and development industry, housing providers and other partners to increase housing supply and build on the momentum created through HAF.

Learn more at London.CA/morehomes .

stories.title: The Wild Child returns: From Maine museum back to London, Ont.
stories.summary: Car enthusiasts were given a special treat Saturday when an iconic drag racer made its return to its original home.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Car enthusiasts were given a special treat Saturday when an iconic drag racer made its return to its original home. The ‘Wild Child’ was a legendary 1965 Ford Falcon B/FX (Factory Experimental) drag racer campaigned by London’s Rankin Ford dealership.

Current owner Joe Germann brought the car to display at the East London Timing Association car show Saturday. “Ford of Canada decided to build some BFX race cars (in 1965),” said Germann. “They built three B/FX race cars with 289 HiPo (High Performance 89 cubic-inch, small-block V8) in them, nine-inch rear end, Nascar top loader, fiberglass body parts and things of that nature of this date.

One of them is completely gone and the other one is just the shell. So, this is the only car of those that were built up here to be race cars that is alive.” The car was acquired by Rankin Ford in May 1965 and driven by local racers Ev Rowse and John McIntyre at Canadian tracks like Grand Bend, Cayuga, and St.

Thomas, as well as throughout the U.S. It piled up a string of victories in its successful debut in the Nhra’s B/FX class in 1965, running in the 11.50s at about 120 mph. “It was brand new and it was pretty damn exciting,” said Rowse of Dorchester.

“It was a nice ride, and it could go like hell and make a lot of noise.” In 1965, Rankin Ford held a contest in the newspaper to name the vehicle. The winner received $25. “It was a local car that did well on the bigger screen,” said Dave Mathers, one of the few people who have owned the vehicle.

“Some of the national events it went to, and it did well. It won a bunch of races, and it was good advertising for Rankin Ford at the time as well.” Mathers is one of six people who have owned the vehicle since 1965. “At the end of the 1967 season, Rankin decided they’d had enough, so they sold the car to Bob Jezquel from Woodstock,” said Mathers.

“Bob kept it till 1993 when I bought it and I restored back to one of the original colours. A guy came in (to the showroom where Mathers displayed it) and offered me a lot of money for the car, so I sold it to him. He sold it to another guy, and then that guy sold it to Joe.” Germann is from Boston and has kept the car at both his home and in the Owls Head Transportation Museum in Maine.

He had no idea the history of the car, when he bought it in auction in 2003. “I’d been looking for a ‘Cammer’ motor, (Overhead-Cam 427-cu.in. V-8 engine, also known as the Sohc),” said Germann. “I found the car, and I didn’t know the history.

I found out about Ev Rowse, John McIntyre, some years later. I restored the car back to what it was originally. The only difference and a difference in the restoration was in ‘67, they put the stock motor in it and painted the car blue.

I didn’t want the car blue. I wanted it the ‘Wild Child’ red. So, we painted it the (original) ‘Wild Child’ red.” Saturday, Rowse – a Canadian Drag Racing Hall of Famer- was able to see the car again. “I’m pretty proud of Joe,” said Rowse.

“The work he’s done and the way this car looks today, it’s fantastic. It’s just gorgeous.” Germann brings has brought the car back to its original home a few times over the past 23 years. He often takes it out on the track but wasn’t able to this time because of the rain Friday.

“We come back every few years, and it’s nice to come back and see our old friends,” said Germann.

stories.title: Temporary road closures for culvert replacements
stories.summary: The City of London will be undertaking culvert replacements this summer and into the fall which will mean temporary road closures as the work
stories.content:
The City of London will be undertaking culvert replacements this summer and into the fall which will mean temporary road closures as the work gets underway. This work is being done primarily in the southeast and southwest parts of the city.

The culvert replacement program will take place at the following locations and dates:

Westdel Bourne between Sharon Road and Longwoods Road - August 10 to August 14

Scotland Drive between Morrison Road and White Oak Road - August 31 to September 4

Scotland Drive between Old Victoria Road and Westchester Bourne (Middlesex County) - September 8 to September 12

Scotland Drive between Wellington Road South and Highbury Avenue South - September 21 to September 28

Scotland Drive between White Oak Road and Wellington Road South - September 28 to October 5

Sharon Road at Murray Road - October 5 to October 13

Westminster Drive between Highbury Avenue South and Old Victoria Road - October 19 to October 26

What is a culvert?

A culvert is a structure that allows water to pass under or around infrastructure, such as a road or railroad. Culverts help prevent flooding, minimize erosion, and maintain roads in good condition longer.

Why is this happening now?

Repairs and replacement in the near term are required to ensure structural integrity, address safety hazards, protect infrastructure from damage due to stream water fluctuation and precipitation runoff, prevent upstream flooding, and ensure compliance with environmental standards.

Transportation impacts

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Please follow the detour signage. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Above: A map showing the culvert replacement locations on Westdel Bourne and Sharon Road in the southwest part of the city.

Above: A map showing the project areas for the culvert replacements in the southeast end of the city.

You can learn more on Renew London .

stories.title: Historic Model T Fords drive into London for 69th Annual International Tour
stories.summary: The streets of London, Ont. are echoing with the distinctive rumble of a bygone era as the 69th Annual Model T Ford Club International Tour, dubbed the Thames Valley Tour, has officially rolled into town.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The streets of London, Ont. are echoing with the distinctive rumble of a bygone era as the 69th Annual Model T Ford Club International Tour, dubbed the Thames Valley Tour, has officially rolled into town. From July 19 to July 24, 2026, the city and the surrounding southwestern Ontario region are playing host to approximately 150 of the finest remaining examples of the first automobile to truly bring personal transportation to the masses.

Organized by the Ontario Region Model T Ford Club, which is also celebrating its 50th anniversary this year, the prestigious international event has drawn an estimated 350 to 400 enthusiasts from across Canada, the United States, and Australia.

The Ford Model T, produced between 1908 and 1927, is legendary for its role in transforming society. “This is the car that Henry Ford developed. So, everybody had a mode of transportation,” explained Brian Dowell, who brought a meticulously restored Model T from Saint Clair, MI., for the event.

Mark Schneider, tour co-chair, elaborated on its revolutionary impact, “This was the first vehicle they would have ever owned. They were literally showing up at the dealership in horses and buggies and leaving with the Model T.” The tour is not just a gathering of vintage cars; it’s a celebration of automotive heritage and the dedication of owners who preserve these icons.

Many vehicles on display have undergone extensive, painstaking restorations. Eric MacLeod’s sedan, one of two competing for the coveted Stynoski Award for the most meticulously restored Model T, has a remarkable history.

“My dad bought it as a high school student in 1952. It was in a junkyard,” MacLeod shared. Judges meticulously examine every component, from nuts and bolts to original tools and manuals to determine the winner. The passion for these automobiles extends beyond mechanical restoration.

Some participants embrace the spirit of the era by dressing in period attire. Nicolette and Joel Merlesmith, who arrived from Virginia with their 1920 Model T, believe in fully immersing themselves in the experience. “You’re driving around in vintage vehicles.

Why not look the part?” Nicolette commented. Their own car has a dramatic backstory; Joel recounted how Nicolette’s grandfather intervened to save the vehicle from being rolled down a hill into a dump. After decades sitting in a barn, it has recently been brought back to life by the Merlesmiths over the past two years.

Philanthropist Steve Plunkett, a car enthusiast himself, expressed his delight in hosting the Model Ts at his estate in west London. “It won’t be back here again. So, this is sort of a once in a lifetime,” he noted, recognizing the unique opportunity.

The tour is designed to showcase the region’s charm, with participants following planned routes through London and its surrounding communities. They will be exploring scenic back roads, visiting local businesses, museums, and attractions throughout Middlesex and Perth counties.

“Every stop, every gas stop is a mini car show,” said MacLeod, highlighting the camaraderie and constant admiration these vehicles generate. Owners note that while restorations demand significant passion and investment, keeping the vehicles running mechanically is surprisingly straightforward.

With an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 Model Ts still in existence worldwide, events like the Thames Valley Tour are crucial in keeping the legacy of this groundbreaking automobile alive for future generations. The tour concludes on Friday, July 24.

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: After making 54 donations, Elizabeth Peloza reflects on receiving the gift of life
stories.summary: As a regular donor at Canadian Blood Services, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has given the gift of life to others. She now knows firsthand what it also means to receive.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
As a regular donor at Canadian Blood Services, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has given the gift of life to others. She now knows firsthand what it also means to receive. Peloza is sharing her experiences during chemotherapy treatments in a CTV News series called ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’ On the morning of April 29, she recorded a brief video inside the London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) explaining that she would require a blood transfusion while being treated for pneumonia.

“My doctor asked if I had ever received a blood transfusion. I need to receive one because my hemoglobin levels are low,” she said into her phone. Peloza then reflected on the significance of the moment. “I’ve been honored to have been 54 times a Canadian Blood Services donor.

This is my first transfusion. So humbly, thank you to those who donate,” she said. The blood transfusion helped save her life and maintain her schedule chemotherapy treatments. A month and a half later, she visited the Canadian Blood Services donation centre at 820 Wharncliffe Rd.

S. in recognition of National Blood Donor Week. Her chemotherapy treatments prevent Peloza from donating, but she held her donor ID card in her hand, proudly glancing at the large 50 printed on its face — knowing fully what it represents.

“When summer vacation comes, people go out of the town, [they] reprioritize things, and the donations drop, but the demand stays the same. So, it’s really important to schedule those appointments,” she explained. “Canadian Blood Services needs to welcome over a million new donors by 2030, and the reason is the need for blood is increasing by 10 per cent, and plasma by 50 per cent,” explained Marisa Gatfield, community development manager at Canadian Blood Services.

National Blood Donor Week runs from June 8 to 14. “It’s actually moving to have the councillor here right now,” said David House, who spoke with Peloza while making his weekly plasma donation. “It’s very nice to know it’s going to help real people.” “The need for blood is constant, and you never know when you’re going to need it, or someone that you know May need blood or a blood product,” Gatfield said.

“I’m grateful for Elizabeth being here and sharing her journey with others, and inspiring others to step-up and become a donor.” A few years ago, blood plasma donations also saved Peloza’s son. “I was donating then, and along the way my son had become ill with GBS (Guillain-Barré syndrome) and for that, the only cure is human plasma donation,” she explained.

“So, we were already gifted that his life was saved with blood products.” “We did a donor drive after that to get more awareness, and I became really meticulous about donating,” Peloza recalled. But now it’s her inability to continue repaying the gift of life that saved her son that makes visiting the donation centre tough for the mom of three.

“I miss it. It’s an opportunity I can’t take right now and it’s going to be years until I can take that again,” Peloza says. “So, I really want to make this a public call for all those donations I would be doing weekly. I need people to step in to help fill my seat, and the seats of those who want to donate — but can’t.

Booking an appointment to make a donation can be done online, by calling 1-888-2-Donate, or on the GiveBlood app.

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Elizabeth Peloza discovers how a Look Good Feel Better workshop supports cancer patients
stories.summary: Since undergoing breast cancer surgery last December, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has been sharing her healthcare journey during chemotherapy in a CTV News series titled ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Since undergoing breast cancer surgery last December, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has been sharing her healthcare journey during chemotherapy in a CTV News series titled ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’ Previous rounds of chemo triggered hair loss, then a recent change to her medications caused her eyebrows and eyelashes to fall out.

Peloza turned to the Look Good Feel Better (Lgfb) workshop for cancer patients offered inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC). “Makeup’s never been a strong suit for me,” she admitted.

“So, when the many visual changes started happening to me, I was definitely out of my depth about how to address them. So, I signed up for the Look Good Feel Better workshop.” Look Good Feel Better is Canada’s only national charitable program dedicated to helping people manage the appearance-related impacts of cancer and its treatment.

“We offer a free hair and cosmetic workshop for patients with cancer, and we help them with the appearance-related side effects,” Cottell explained. But the impact of the workshop extends well beyond makeup techniques. “When participants come in, they’re very quiet and shy.

They’re not talking a whole lot [because] they don’t know other women who have cancer,” Cottell explained. “After two hours, it’s truly magical what happens in that room. The women are all talking, sharing different stories, and they all leave with a smile on their face.” Peloza understands.

“You just feel so terrible inside, and sometimes you let that reflect on your outside,” she said about the side effects of her chemo treatments. As Cottell applied makeup to Peloza’s face, her instructions included many words of kindness and compassion.

“You have such beautiful blue eyes,” she told Peloza while rubbing a disposable makeup sponge into an eyeshadow compact. Cottell then warned against reusable makeup brushes during chemotherapy because they can harbour bacteria.

Later while applying blush on Peloza’s cheek, she offered this instruction, “I want you to smile. So that’s the best part of putting that [blush] on your cheek. You get to smile into the mirror.” She also asked Peloza about her moisturizing routine to address the extremely dry skin brought on by chemotherapy.

“It’s wonderful to see the transformation in people,” Cottell said while examining Peloza’s drawn-in eyebrows. “And it does give them confidence. If you’re not feeling well one day, just a quick lipstick, blush and eyebrows get you out the door and you feel really good.” At the end, Peloza smiled as she gazed in a mirror at the results of her makeup workshop.

She spoke candidly to Cottell, “I’ll probably start to care more once I can actually go back out in public. I’ve been kind of isolating after the pneumonia and hospitalized for a week.” Earlier Cottell had explained that the workshops are an opportunity for cancer patients to speak with others who know firsthand what they’re going through.

Cottell is herself a cancer survivor. “I personally have had cancer, and I can tell you that all of the other women that have gone through this program helped me when I had mine,” she said. “As you go through treatment and so many things change, you might isolate more because you don’t feel as confident in yourself,” Peloza explained.

“You don’t bother to [apply makeup] like you used to. So, it’s getting that back and being reminded that you are still you - and you are still beautiful.” Cottell hopes more cancer patients will try the workshop saying, “We really would like to get the word out because so many patients don’t know about it.” National skincare and makeup brands donate the products given to each workshop participant, and they include shades for all skin tones.

Lgfb also offers special online workshops for teens with cancer. Details about the program and upcoming workshops (in-person or online) can be found on the Look Good Feel Better website.

stories.title: Community bike riding event returns to London
stories.summary: The Forest City Slow Roll takes place on June 6, with cyclist of all level ride through London neighborhoods. ...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
The Forest City Slow Roll takes place on June 6, with cyclist of all level ride through London neighborhoods.

This year’s London Cycle Link ride will go through six different neighborhoods, including two new additions: old south and SoHo Laura Galvis Daza said the organizer of the event.

“Our mission is to celebrate the bicycle,” Galvis Daza said. “To encourage active transportation and pedestrian-first and cycling infrastructure in London.”

The ride will also showcase major biking projects along Central Ave, Colborne, Ridout Street, and the newly opened Victoria Street Bridge, Galvis Daza said. As well to enjoy the historical infrastructures the city has to offer.

“Streets are meant for people. It’s pedestrians, cyclists, motorists, all abilities young and old, and we need to continue finding ways to share our streets” she said.

The idea for the slow roll began in 2022, when the Forest City Cycling Challenge approached London Cycle Link after seeing similar events in other cities and proposed a partnership.

London Cycle Link is a charitable organization that helps Londoners ride more. It was established in 2013, then launched a community bike repair shop in 2017, and added an education program in 2021. They advocate for safer streets at all levels of government and nurture a thriving cycling culture in London, Galvis Daza said.

“It’s a lot of work setting up an event like this, especially in downtown London. It took about seven months to organize,” said Galvis Daza.

The event runs from 1 p.m. to 6 p.m., with the ride starting at 3 p.m. on Dundas Street between Ridout and Talbot Street. Riders are encouraged to dress up. Food trucks, prizes, and activities will be available before and after for all those who register online.

Due to the amount of work involved, there is no rain date. Organizers say the event will proceed in all weather, with tents available if needed.

Currently there’s more than 300 participants with a capacity of 500 riders. Registration is free online for those interested.

Galvis Daza also thanked all sponsors, volunteers, vendors, and riders for making the event possible.

Due to the amount of work involved, there is no rain date. Organizers say the event will proceed in all weather, with tents available if needed.
Currently there’s more than 300 participants with a capacity of 500 riders. Registration is free online for those interested.
Galvis Daza also thanked all sponsors, volunteers, vendors, and riders for making the event possible.

stories.title: 12 people displaced after townhouse fire
stories.summary: *This story was updated on June 4, 2026 Twelve people have been displaced as a result of this week's fire at a...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
*This story was updated on June 4, 2026

Twelve people have been displaced as a result of this week’s fire at a north London townhouse complex, firefighters said.

The blaze damaged three units from the complex on Silverbrook Drive, but could have been worse if not for working smoke detectors, the London Fire Department (LFD) said in a post on social media.

Fire crews responded to multiple 911 calls early Wednesday morning, firefighters said. When they arrived around 1 a.m., firefighters saw multiple units flames and smoke pouring out of mutltiple unites in the back of one of the homes.

“Firefighters acted quickly to knock down the fire and successfully limit the extension to the adjacent units,” London Fire Department said in a post on X.

No civilians were reported injured, but one firefighter sustained minor injuries, LFD. The cause of the fire has not been determined but is under investigation, firefighters said.

“Today’s townhouse fire serves as an important reminder of the critical role working smoke detectors play in protecting lives,” they said in the post on X. “Early warning smoke detectors provides valuable time to escape – this is especially important in multi-unit dwellings were fire and smoke can quickly affect neighbouring units.”

Initially the damages were estimated to be over $1 million dollars, but since the initial statement the estimate has decreased to $800,000.

stories.title: ‘When the sun is shining, it’s very busy’; How beautiful weather effects golf courses
stories.summary: Weather can make or break a golfer's day on the course. With the warmer weather London golf courses' time shee...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Weather can make or break a golfer’s day on the course. With the warmer weather London golf courses’ time sheets are filling up.

“I’m thankful, since winter was so cold it’s very nice to have this sun” said Jean whose been golfing for eight years.

“It’s beautiful out here, it was a slow start only on my seventh round this year, but great weather no humidity” said Jeff Van Geel a golfer for 42 years.

“Its very good weather considering the start of the season, but it’s very good” said Jeff’s wife Sylvie who has been golfing with him for 11 years.

Bitter cold winds and rain in the early spring always hurts the club house at the start of golf season, but it builds up the eagerness of the golfers to get out there.

“You never want a damp April because you’ll see a little dip in sales, but it builds the hunger for everyone once the weather turns” said Rob Vincent the professional supervisor at Fanshawe Golf Course.

Owners have been very lucky this year with how the weather is treating the golf courses. Even when it’s bad, diehard fans come out to fill up those spots.

“We have quite a few passholders between the two sites that are going to play rain or shine” Vincent said “But the diehards will play when it’s 2 C and raining.”

He added that golf as a whole has been growing in popularity at a rapid rate. After COVID-19 people who would normally play a couple times per week now come up to five times, and the dedicated golfers who were four times are coming almost everyday. Vincent has been with the city for 20 years watching the growth of golf first hand.

“When we were reopening the world all you could do was get gas, get groceries and play golf, there were no soccer leagues, couldn’t play tennis, and all the gyms were closed” Vincent stated. “2022 was a good year, I expected for numbers to go down, but it was the opposite. I think people saw how great the game is and they stuck around.”

Vincent has been golfing for nearly 35 years. He said golf relaxing for his mind, gets him away from screens, and meeting with your friends.

stories.title: ‘Most powerful protest, is love’: Fanshawe reveals new permanent pride symbol
stories.summary: Fanshawe revealed the newly painted sidewalk in commemoration of Pride Month and commitment for a safe communi...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Fanshawe revealed the newly painted sidewalk in commemoration of Pride Month and commitment for a safe community.

“ This sidewalk is a reminder that we are walking on ground that is shaped by courage” said Joseph Pazzano, Executive Director of Student Wellbeing. It was revealed at the London campus’ annual flag raising ceremony on June 1.

“The sidewalk is near the flag poles at the London campus, and the regional campuses will have a framed pride flag to symbolize our strong commitment for the community” said Xieling Zhang the Centre for Edi’s Consultant at Fanshawe.

“We’re not just focusing on one campus but trying all the regional campuses.”

The ceremonies have taken place on June 1 and June 2 with London and Simcoe on the 1st, and St. Thomas and Woodstock on the 2nd.

“I t’s a way for Fanshawe College to display that visible symbol and also a commitment to creating really safe , affirming and inclusive spaces for all students and employees” said Zhang.

The progress pride flag is the symbol of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, the flag has changed a lot over the years adding colours for the trans, intersex, black, indigenous, and people of colour communities.

“N ot only represents the strength and history that the que er commun ity has, but it s howcases the communit y that comes together regardless of gender, sex, love, all of that is more of those family vibes that the queer community brings together” said Veronica Royale a drag queen in London.

Royale has been performing as a drag queen in London for seven years, appearing in shows that support local charities such as Y.O.U. and St. Leonard’s. Through these performances, she helps raise funds for community organizations while also bringing greater visibility to drag culture and the broader queer community.

June 1 marks the start of pride month for the 2SLGBTQIA+ community that celebrates the pride and contributions of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community.

stories.title: London house fire is under investigation after $500k in damage
stories.summary: Crews responded at about 1:30 a.m. Friday to the 300 block of Grey Street for a structure fire. Firefighters e...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Crews responded at about 1:30 a.m. Friday to the 300 block of Grey Street for a structure fire.

Firefighters encountered heavy smoke and flames on arrival.

Crews initially launched an offensive attack but were pulled back by command due to structural instability. Firefighters then switched to a defensive aerial attack.

This incident comes four days after a former church caught fire, that took place down the road on Wellington Street near Grey Street.

All crews have been cleared from the scene. No injuries were reported. Damage is estimated at more than $500,000.

stories.title: Beekeeping program has started at Fanshawe
stories.summary: Fanshawe College has launched a new beekeeping program this summer. The program works with the college's apiar...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Fanshawe College has launched a new beekeeping program this summer.

The program works with the college’s apiary, located near the baseball diamonds on campus.

Fanshawe’s apiary is monitored by a dedicated beekeeper. Visitors are welcome but must obtain permission, as the area is fenced off.

The course consists of a mix of in-class learning and regular lectures that are highly interactive, along with time in the apiary, where students apply what they have learned in practice, said Graham Thompson, a professor in the program.

“I think a lot of people who are interested in beekeeping and might consider taking this course think that bees are interesting, or cute, or admirable, but it’s not exactly 100 per cent certain what that interest is,” said Thompson.

May 20 marks World Bee Day, which raises awareness of the important role bees and other pollinators play in the ecosystem and the challenges they face.

Students also learn about the biology and evolution of bees, as well as the cultures and history associated with beekeeping.

“Fanshawe is a little more thorough, with a lot of contact time spread out over the summer. There are classes starting in the spring, another group in June and another at the end of July. That’s meant to roughly capture the different seasons and the bee cycle,” said Thompson.

“When you learn how their societies function, I think that’s the jaw-dropper. People are sitting at the dinner table after the course saying, ‘You would not believe what I learned about bees today,’” he added.

Beekeepers’ hives not only produce honey, but are also used to pollinate crops at certain times of the year. These are called pollination services and play a major role for farmers.

stories.title: E-bike cyclist killed in east London
stories.summary: An investigation is underway after an e-bike rider died following a collision with a vehicle in east London la...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
An investigation is underway after an e-bike rider died following a collision with a vehicle in east London last week.

According to a news release from London police, emergency crews were called around 3 p.m. on May 15 to a crash involving an e-bike and a vehicle near Brydges Street and Egerton Street.

Police say the cyclist was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died.

The driver remained at the scene.

Members of the London Police Service’s road safety section are investigating.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 2:45 p.m. and 3:10 p.m. on May 15, and who May have witnessed the crash or has dashcam or surveillance footage, to contact police.

stories.title: Human Trafficking is evolving with Technology and AI
stories.summary: Human traffickers are using artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology, to exploit and control their vi...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Human traffickers are using artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology, to exploit and control their victims in London, says an anti-violence advocate. New tactics include tracking victims remotely and threatening to release pornographic photos and videos that May not be real, said Jessie Rodger who is the executive director of Anova in London.

“It’s not unusual to hear victims and survivors say that their phone or house is bugged and that they’re being surveilled or tracked,” said Rodger. Gender-based-violence workers have also heard about cases of “financial abuse,” which includes the perpetrator adding debt to a victim’s account, they said.

“These (tactics) all keep the abuser connected with the victim in some way,” they said. “It’s important to pay attention and to learn so we can keep up with how traffickers and perpetrators of violence are using new forms of technology control or violate the people that they’re abusing.”

The comments come amid concerns about sex trafficking in London. Earlier this month, police published the photo of a Scarborough man they’d arrested on human trafficking charges, saying they believe there May be additional victims in London.

In that case, London Police said they had been contacted by a woman who said she had been directed to provide sexual services to clients in multiple Ontario cities.

London has been called a “hub” for human trafficking because its location along Highway 401 between Detroit and Toronto makes it convenient to place and move women in and out of hotels. Police say perpetrators look for people who have specific traits and circumstances.

“They look for vulnerable people that are not happy in their current life or situation, offer them a better option, make it sound like they want to be friends and maybe a boyfriend situation and we call that a ‘Romeo Pimp’ where they buy them treats nice gifts, and take them on dates, which then transitions to the trafficking” said Det. Insp. Jennifer Noel with London Police Services.

Teens and young women especially should know there are people out there who May try to exploit them for sex trafficking, Noel said. “If something seems too good to be true, it probably is, she said.

“Human Trafficking often takes place throughout Ontario, people who exploit women in trafficking move from city to city frequently, sometimes without consent.”

LPS also works with other Ontario services with an integrated joint forces team with help from the Ontario government to make sure the other services work together with the constant moving of human trafficking.

If you or someone you know who is struggling with violence, trauma, or need support, call Anova’s help line open 24/7 at 519-642-3000
