LPS also works with other Ontario services with an integrated joint forces team with help from the Ontario government to make sure the other services work together with the constant moving of human trafficking.
If you or someone you know who is struggling with violence, trauma, or need support, call Anova’s help line open 24/7 at 519-642-3000

stories.title: Mortgage broker behind popular billboards reveals his operation
stories.summary: If you've travelled across London, you probably have seen more than one Mike Hattim billboard around the city....
stories.content:
If you’ve travelled across London, you probably have seen more than one Mike Hattim billboard around the city.

And you’ve probably noticed his billboard costumes are always changing, depending on what people are talking about or what holiday is coming up. One day he’s up there in a superhero cape, another day he’s sporting bunny ears or parodying your favourite reality TV show.

Until fairly recently, the mortgage broker focused his creativity and graphic design background on digital ads.

“Then I said, you know, why don’t we try something different,” he said.

It almost didn’t happen. A few days before The Broker was scheduled to go up, Hattim called his rep at Pattison Outdoor Advertising Billboards to say he had buyer’s remorse. It was a terrible idea, he thought.

“She’s like, ‘no, no, it’s amazing,'” Hattim recalled. “ You’re going to love it.”

The billboard got a lot of response after it was put up. And while not all responses were positive, he liked that people were talking.

“Y ou got a guy selling cars, he’s got a car advertisement, you know, real estate, mortgages, you name the industry,” said Hattim, who has been a mortgabe broker for 23 years and works with Dominion Lending Centres. He started to ask, “If it’s a sales perspective, it’s how can I become a little bit more noticeable?”

The way Hattim gets more noticeable is by doing something that stands out; in more ways than one. For example, you can often see six identical versions of his latest billboard beside each other at Wortley Road and Stanley Street.

Mixed reactions for his billboards can be found all over social media.

“Mike Hattim, please chill,” said one thread on Reddit that shows the group of six billboards adorned by Hattim in a superhero cape.

“I am begging you to chill on the billboard ads. I cannot escape them,” wrote the user scorpio_sunshine98. “The love island-inspired ad you did last summer is etched into my mind in a bad way. . . It’s a lot to take in at 8am on the way to work. I urge you to dial it back.”

But while the thread drew 171 comments, many of them urged Hattim to continue.

“neverchill,” wrote one user. “You make me smile when I see these,” wrote another.

Mike Hattim, please chill by u/scorpio_sunshine98 in londonontario

Hattim said he does most of the work to come up wtih the billboards and Pattison’s team also helps.

Every year when Hattim restarts his billboard campaign, they brainstorm ideas of what to do. He makes sure to hit the holiday billboards including Christmas, Valentines day, and more related to special months.

Most of these designs are made in Photoshop by Hattim as he learned the software in school.

These are some more designs Mike used over the years:

Hattim’s biggest design was his parody on the show Love Island. According to his analytics, it had the biggest response through online activity.

According to Hattim, many of his designs don’t get noticed and not everything works.

He says some designs even don’t make the cut or they are on the edge of being implemented. Hattim says he gives it a shot anyways.

While Hattim does have a presence on social media , he says the billboards have been the most expensive and the most successful option.

“It’s one of those options where you don’t go out and just do one for a few months and that’s the end of it,” said Hattim. “ It’s a commitment long term, just like a commercial or a radio commercial or TV commercial, any of those things. You need long term viewership in order for it to start to maintain and bring back some value. So it’s a heavy initial investment.”

Hattim budgets around $10,000 a month, depending on the time of year and what is happening.

The budget is towards 15 to 20 billboards, ranging from month to month.

Hattim says he is now noticing the effect of the billboards to his business after nine years. People initially for a few years acknowledged the billboards and say something to Hattim.

Now when people book appointments with Hattim, He says 9 out of 10 people bring up these creative billboards. Many seeing them years in advance and contacting mike when they need him.

In addition to being a mortgage broker, Hattim is a proud supporter of the Humane Society. He was also an advocate for the most recent London location on Dundas Street, east of Highbury.

Hattim also supports the Cancer Foundation and local GoFundMe’s.

For those who have gone to Basha Lebanese Restobar on Hyde Park, you May have seen a drink on the menu called “The Mike Hattim.” The drink was named after him as his cousin owns the restaurant.

As a nod to his past, Hattim has an Imdb page for two movies he executive produced for. Mike says it was not glamourous as he had friends in the film industry and they were “more or less investments.”

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza on the toll of chemotherapy and importance of community
stories.summary: Following breast cancer surgery, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is chronicling her experiences during chemotherapy in a CTV News series called Healing in the Public Eye.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Following breast cancer surgery, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is chronicling her experiences during chemotherapy in a CTV News series called Healing in the Public Eye. This week, Peloza held a community meeting in her ward for the first time since speaking publicly about undergoing cancer surgery and chemotherapy treatments.

There were opportunities for residents to meet with representatives from City Hall, London police, and other local agencies about issues in south London. But many in her community showed up just to offer encouragement. Initially intending to keep a safe distance because her immune system is temporarily compromised, she was soon accepting hug after hug.

“It has been really isolating,” Peloza admitted about chemotherapy. “It’s nice that you hear people sharing their stories, that they can relate. That [sharing my story] is helping them understand if somebody in their life has [cancer].” Penny Moore has been battling thyroid cancer for 25 years and arrived early to the ward meeting to lend her support.

“Some days you don’t think you’re going to get through it, but you do” Moore explained. “The thing is [Peloza’s] getting the awareness [of early cancer screening] out there.” Former City Councillor and long-term cancer survivor Harold Usher greeted Peloza with a hug.

“I had prostate cancer before I became a city councillor. I also had colon cancer 10 years later and for that I had chemotherapy,” Usher recalled. “I admire Elizabeth for doing this because she’s saying to people that this is what might happen, [so] don’t be afraid.

I want to live. So I’m going to take whatever necessary steps to live longer.” Severe side effects from the chemotherapy threatened Peloza’s attendance, but she persevered. “I was looking forward to seeing everybody, having not gathered as a community since treatment started,” she said.

“But symptom management wise, it has not been a good couple of days. I’m back to having the throat pain and not wanting to swallow because it feels a bit like sandpaper and glass.” Her next chemotherapy treatment will be her fifth of eight, but it’s the first with a different drug that will cause more painful side effects.

“We switch next Friday. In my mind, all bets are off. I know it’s going to involve bone pain,” she said with a smile, masking her apprehension with humour. She will be speaking with her oncologist about pain management. “Bone pain, there’s medication for it, and I think people understand it a little bit better with pain management,” she added.

In the meantime, Peloza is happy to have connected with her community before the difficult second half of her chemotherapy treatments. “Knowing that the medication was going to be switching, it was really important to host this meeting with community now, when I can manage the symptoms and still plan to be here,” she said.

“I don’t know what next week’s going to look like after chemo.” But she remains optimistic, “I’m still here and [the] community still gathers.” Share your thoughts and questions via email at AskCTVLondon@bellmedia.CA Selected emails to CTV News will become part of an upcoming segment of Coun.

stories.title: Fanshawe radio students sign off from 106.9 The X after final broadcast
stories.summary: Fanshawe College radio students signed off from 106. 9. The X was for the last time at 10 a.m. Thursday, after...
stories.content:
Fanshawe College radio students signed off from 106. 9. The X was for the last time at 10 a.m. Thursday, after completing what May be the station’s final live broadcast.

The show marked the end of a nearly 50-year era for Cixx-FM, which launched in 1978 as Canada’s first licensed campus radio station dedicated to teaching broadcast radio and journalism students.

Last year, Fanshawe announced that it was suspending the station because it couldn’t afford to run it any longer. But earlier this year, the college accepted a proposal from a London community nonprofit named WeRise , which is now exploring ways to keep the station running.

For Fanshawe radio and media production students, Thursday’s morning show was emotional, marking the end of years spent learning live radio and building on-air experience.

“It’s become like a family to me,” said Emily Slagter, a graduating student in the program. “It felt like a space where I could be creative and understand how a real radio station works.”

Her peers Julia Seitz and Connor Brooks, who hosted the last live show, highlighted the challenges and learning moments along the way.

“A lot of firsts… launching songs, forgetting to turn on the mic, even making mistakes on air,” Seitz said.

Brooks said being part of the station’s history made the experience meaningful.

“I’m incredibly privileged to sit in a chair that so many other broadcasters have sat in,” he said.

Over the past 50 years, many producers, journalists and broadcasters have gotten their start behind the mic of 106.9 The X .

During the show, Brooks and Seitz thanked Fanshawe staff, instructors and listeners for their support throughout the program.

“None of this happens if you’re not out there listening,” Brooks said.

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza’s unplanned hospitalization and a gift of warmth from Victoria’s Quilts Canada
stories.summary: As she undergoes chemotherapy treatment following breast cancer surgery, London City Councillor and Budget Chair Elizabeth Peloza is documenting her health journey on CTV News.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
“It’s about offering comfort and warmth, especially because anyone who’s gone through it knows chemo is cold,” explained Ellen James, a quilter who also helps acquire donated fabric and batting. “The rooms are cold, so it’s nice to have something to wrap-up in and be comfortable.

Also to know that someone cares enough to do this for them.” The volunteer group relies entirely on donations to create and deliver up to 32 quilts each month to people with cancer. Jan Devereux emphasizes that volunteers don’t need to be quilters.

Like her, some offer their time delivering completed quilts, assisting the board, and promoting their mission of providing comfort to people with cancer. “It’s so grassroots,” Devereux added. “It’s such a good cause that I felt I needed to get involved.” James added, “A week after my nephew passed away from cancer, a friend of mine and I decided that we were going to become involved.” The pair presented a quilt to Peloza ahead of her fourth chemotherapy treatment.

“There’s people across Canada who are doing this,” Peloza explained about the organization. “Maybe they’ve been touched by cancer, maybe someone in their family has been touched by cancer, maybe they just want to help.” Peloza reads the patch stitched onto every completed quilt, “Victoria’s Quilts Canada.

We hope this quilt brings you comfort and support in this difficult time. You are not alone.” The message comes a week after Peloza acknowledged she feels lonely and isolated because chemotherapy has temporarily compromised her immune system.

“When you’re sitting there getting chemo, you know that the bad days are about to start,” she said. “So to have something reminding you that you’re in someone’s thoughts, knowing you are not alone is going to be a huge help.” A dedicated group of quilters at all skill levels meet monthly at Wesley Knox United Church in London and take the quilts home to finish.

There is no cost for people with cancer to receive a quilt. Peloza is moved by their dedication, “It’s a gift of love from someone who doesn’t even know you.” Meanwhile, Peloza is sharing a medical scare that recently landed her in hospital overnight.

“My Easter was not as intended. I had to spend Saturday evening and Sunday morning in the emergency department,” she recalled. Chemotherapy has made some of her skin and tissues prone to bleed. “From blowing my nose, it sometimes bleeds.

I managed to get an infection,” she explained. Days after leaving the hospital, she was still worried about the consequences to her chemotherapy schedule. Having to spend time around potentially contagious illnesses inside the hospital’s ED was her initial concern, but the treatment of the sinus infection led to another, “[I’m] apprehensive.

I got IV antibiotics at the hospital and got some more antibiotics to take orally. Otherwise, her chemotherapy will be paused. “This Friday would be round four of eight, so this is almost my halfway point. I have months ahead. Like her, some offer their time delivering completed quilts, assisting the board, and promoting their mission of providing comfort to people with cancer. “It’s so grassroots,” Devereux added. “It’s such a good cause that I felt I needed to get involved.” James added, “A week after my nephew passed away from cancer, a friend of mine and I decided that we were going to become involved.” The pair presented a quilt to Peloza ahead of her fourth chemotherapy treatment.

stories.title: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza: Wig and Turban Boutique highlights impact of volunteers and donations
stories.summary: Since her second chemotherapy treatment, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is facing a side effect she knew was coming. Her hair is falling out.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Since her second chemotherapy treatment, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is facing a side effect she knew was coming. Her hair is falling out. “Your sink is full [of hair]. You get up and your pillow is covered,” she told CTV News while seating inside the Wig and Turban Boutique at the London Health Sciences Centre’s Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre.

“So, it was time for this. I’m really grateful today to come in for this opportunity,” Peloza explained. The city councillor and city hall budget chair is receiving chemotherapy after undergoing breast cancer surgery in December.

She arrived admitting it had been a tough morning but was determined to shine a light on the specialized care being provided in a small corner of the region’s cancer centre, and its need for volunteers and donations of synthetic wigs, scarves, and turbans.

IN Photos: Motherhood shaping medical decision IN Photos: Navigating Cancer, Work, and Life “I certainly have never worn a wig before, so learning the process of putting on a cap and then the fit [along] the hairline is something that I really appreciate.

Someone is walking you through it,” she explained. “Last year, we had 1,500 wigs that were borrowed,” said Carol Wilkinson, one of the volunteers who operate the boutique. “They can come and pick out a wig for themselves, or they can also have some turbans,” Wilkinson explained.

“It’s private, in front of a mirror, and they’re often with family members, whether it’s spouses or their children, or girlfriends.” “One of the biggest things you lose in this [chemotherapy] process is your control. There is nothing you are in charge of,” reflected Peloza.

“What you’re wearing for a wig, head scarf, [or] covering and what you do with your appearance, that’s all that’s left.” Wilkinson recalled, “I share the story of a woman who came in who barely got past the door, and she fell apart.

She started to cry. And when I told her how the program worked and that everything was free of charge, she couldn’t believe it because she thought it would cost money.” The free service relies on volunteers and people who donate scarves, turbans, and synthetic wigs.

Wilkinson lost her father to cancer and began volunteering after retirement. “It’s a very intimate experience, so both this volunteer position and my other volunteer position, I feel are an honor for me to be able to help,” Wilkinson explained.

Peloza believes it important to highlight the impact of the boutique and its volunteers, saying, “This is our community giving back. And it’s not just to Londoners; this is a regional facility. It’s given with love and care.” “We have a very committed group of volunteers in the Wig and Turban Boutique, and we’re very fortunate to have them come in on a regular basis,” said LHSC Manager of Volunteer Services Meaghan Innes.

“We always look for extra volunteers who can help with vacations and sick coverage. We also have other volunteer opportunities within the cancer center. We’re happy to receive people who are interested in having those conversations,” she said.

If you’re interested in donating wigs, London Health Sciences Centre recommends the following:

stories.title: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza: How motherhood and her medical decisions are shaping her chemotherapy journey
stories.summary: Following her second chemotherapy treatment, Peloza is sharing her healing journey in an ongoing series on CTV News at 6 p.m. and at CTVNewsLondon.CA
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
On Monday, London Coun. Elizabeth Peloza sat down for an interview about how motherhood and medical decisions are shaping her chemotherapy journey in the wake of breast cancer surgery last December. IN Photos: Motherhood shaping medical decision IN Photos: Navigating Cancer, Work, and Life Peloza is sharing her healing journey in an ongoing series on CTV News at 6 p.m. and at CTVNewsLondon.CA Viewers are invited to share feedback and questions at this email address, AskCTVLondon@bellmedia.CA.

CTV News - How are you balancing being a mom, a city councillor, and ensuring your medical care is a priority? Elizabeth Peloza - Last week was a lot. The Picc [Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter] line was put in. Once it went in, I had to go make sure with an X-ray that everything was exactly where it needed to be.

The next day, I’m back at the hospital for bloodwork and an oncologist appointment. The next day, I was back at the hospital for chemo. Each appointment takes like three [or] four hours. It’s perpetually hockey season as a hockey mom; there’s always hockey going on. [I] just try to find that balance and then try to understand my body and let my body take a rest when it needs.

That might mean having an afternoon nap and doing work emails at 11 p.m. [because] that’s when you feel good. You’re doing resident phone calls in the morning because you’re feeling best, and then you’re back to an afternoon of quiet time.

I miss the community interactions and being at events, so just trying to find a way to still meet with people virtually or accommodate their needs. I’m having to avoid those large gatherings that I love. But 700 people, 1,200 people, probably with chemo and no immune system is not the safest place for me to be right now.

CTV News - Tell me about the role your kids play in motivating you through the difficult parts of chemotherapy? Peloza - I have three kids, aged 15 to 20. I am grateful for the tests that are available. The genetic testing available at no charge.

Some other tests that tell you about the likelihood of it recurring somewhere in your body within 10 years. For me, when the tumor margins came back clear and the lymph nodes came back clear I was anticipating just receiving radiation. [But] when those other tests come back.

The numbers were high for a likely reoccurrence. Higher than I’m comfortable with because I have children [that] I’m still raising. So [I] went the chemotherapy route. Two of the boys shaved their heads, different parts.

So now we’re waiting to see if mom can rock the bald haircut as well as they can. So trying to find the humor in it but really making sure that I do what I can to make sure I am here for my kids as they continue growing.

CTV News - Earlier this week you recorded a cellphone video on your way into the hospital to have a Picc inserted into your arm. What role will it play in your chemotherapy? Peloza - My first round of chemo was done with just a normal IV, but it’s a little bit higher risk for me if there’s a problem with medications [flowing] and the damage it can do to your veins.

So I looked into a Picc line. A Picc line is a longer tube that goes in your arm, delivers [medications] closer to your heart. [I was] a little bit apprehensive about it. Did some research and made a decision. Actually, I un-made that decision, and then re-made it.

CTV News - What ultimately made you decide to get it? Peloza - It means fewer needle stabs for the drugs. You can also have your bloodwork done right out of it. I am going to see how this goes. Was also mindful that once it goes in, you can always have it taken out if it’s not working for you, your lifestyle, or you’re not comfortable with it.

With the first round of chemo, the line didn’t go in easily, they had to wait for an IV specialist to come down, so I was just thinking if I did this on my own terms in advance, then I’m better prepared. I’ll go in with less anxiety through the [chemotherapy] process.

I’m happy to show you if you want to help understand the process. CTV News - How was it inserted? Peloza - It’s [inserted] above your elbow, so it’s nice you still have your full range of motion. They mark a spot with their ultrasounds and it actually goes up through [my upper arm] all the way across my shoulder and to the top of my heart.

And having had breast cancer surgery and the lymph node biopsy, that work was all done on the right side of my body so they chose to put [the Picc] in the other side. The nurse made me what I call a beautiful little sleeping bag.

It can go over it, just to help pad it so you don’t get marks in your arm. Then you can put your [medical] sleeve back on, and it holds it against your body so it not flopping around. Surprisingly, I’ve managed to sleep okay with it.

When I shower it has to stay completely dry. They give you a nice shower bag. CTV News - How important was it to have supportive medical staff help you through the process of having the Picc inserted? Peloza - Agnes was great.

She walked me through the process. Everything’s made sterile when you’re having it put in, and they actually cover you with fabric, including your face. That can be intimidating, [but] Agnes made it into a little tent so I wasn’t claustrophobic in there.

Then [she] had verbal instructions as you went through it. ‘I’m doing this.’ ‘The next part is going to feel like pressure for five seconds.’ Not everyone has good communication skills and it really helps when you are going through that process.

It is intimidating [and] a little bit scary. CTV News - What factors do you consider when making your healthcare decisions? Peloza - You’re making what you believe is the best call for your health based on the information you’re given by doctors and nurses.

That’s been serving me well so far. We’ll see how it goes throughout the chemo journey. Some people don’t or can’t use [a Picc], some do the IV lines, and some actually have a port that goes into their chest. For me, this was a recommendation.

So that’s what we did. CTV News - What has the response been like since you began this CTV News series about your chemotherapy? Peloza - A lot of people assume when you’re in public service that you’re a Political Science grad and you love public speaking and you want to be out there in the media.

I don’t. It is a part of the job that’s inherently important for disseminating information to the public. So when this opportunity came up, [chemotherapy] was going to happen to me regardless. This is my journey. Can I help anyone else face their journey a little bit easier?

Resident feedback and community feedback across the board has been really positive. Sharing their stories, how long they’ve been clear of cancer, or raising some warning flags that they hit along the way to be mindful of.

I appreciate the funny stories and words of encouragement. Community support has been good, and they’ve been asking some different things. Can we cover this or that? Or can I speak [about my breast cancer surgery] because they’re just beginning their journey and can I help them understand what’s coming?

content_blocks.text: On Monday, London Coun. Elizabeth Peloza sat down for an interview about how motherhood and medical decisions are shaping her chemotherapy journey in the wake of breast cancer surgery last December. IN Photos: Motherhood shaping medical decision IN Photos: Navigating Cancer, Work, and Life Peloza is sharing her healing journey in an ongoing series on CTV News at 6 p.m. and at CTVNewsLondon.CA Viewers are invited to share feedback and questions at this email address, AskCTVLondon@bellmedia.CA.

CTV News - How are you balancing being a mom, a city councillor, and ensuring your medical care is a priority? Elizabeth Peloza - Last week was a lot. The Picc [Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter] line was put in. Once it went in, I had to go make sure with an X-ray that everything was exactly where it needed to be.

The next day, I’m back at the hospital for bloodwork and an oncologist appointment. The next day, I was back at the hospital for chemo. Each appointment takes like three [or] four hours. It’s perpetually hockey season as a hockey mom; there’s always hockey going on. [I] just try to find that balance and then try to understand my body and let my body take a rest when it needs.

That might mean having an afternoon nap and doing work emails at 11 p.m. [because] that’s when you feel good. You’re doing resident phone calls in the morning because you’re feeling best, and then you’re back to an afternoon of quiet time.

I miss the community interactions and being at events, so just trying to find a way to still meet with people virtually or accommodate their needs. I’m having to avoid those large gatherings that I love. But 700 people, 1,200 people, probably with chemo and no immune system is not the safest place for me to be right now.

CTV News - Tell me about the role your kids play in motivating you through the difficult parts of chemotherapy? Peloza - I have three kids, aged 15 to 20. I am grateful for the tests that are available. The genetic testing available at no charge.

Some other tests that tell you about the likelihood of it recurring somewhere in your body within 10 years. For me, when the tumor margins came back clear and the lymph nodes came back clear I was anticipating just receiving radiation. [But] when those other tests come back.

The numbers were high for a likely reoccurrence. Higher than I’m comfortable with because I have children [that] I’m still raising. So [I] went the chemotherapy route. Two of the boys shaved their heads, different parts.

So now we’re waiting to see if mom can rock the bald haircut as well as they can. So trying to find the humor in it but really making sure that I do what I can to make sure I am here for my kids as they continue growing.

CTV News - Earlier this week you recorded a cellphone video on your way into the hospital to have a Picc inserted into your arm. What role will it play in your chemotherapy? Peloza - My first round of chemo was done with just a normal IV, but it’s a little bit higher risk for me if there’s a problem with medications [flowing] and the damage it can do to your veins.

So I looked into a Picc line. A Picc line is a longer tube that goes in your arm, delivers [medications] closer to your heart. [I was] a little bit apprehensive about it. Did some research and made a decision. Actually, I un-made that decision, and then re-made it.

CTV News - What ultimately made you decide to get it? Peloza - It means fewer needle stabs for the drugs. You can also have your bloodwork done right out of it. I am going to see how this goes. Was also mindful that once it goes in, you can always have it taken out if it’s not working for you, your lifestyle, or you’re not comfortable with it.

With the first round of chemo, the line didn’t go in easily, they had to wait for an IV specialist to come down, so I was just thinking if I did this on my own terms in advance, then I’m better prepared. I’ll go in with less anxiety through the [chemotherapy] process.

I’m happy to show you if you want to help understand the process. CTV News - How was it inserted? Peloza - It’s [inserted] above your elbow, so it’s nice you still have your full range of motion. They mark a spot with their ultrasounds and it actually goes up through [my upper arm] all the way across my shoulder and to the top of my heart.

And having had breast cancer surgery and the lymph node biopsy, that work was all done on the right side of my body so they chose to put [the Picc] in the other side. The nurse made me what I call a beautiful little sleeping bag.

It can go over it, just to help pad it so you don’t get marks in your arm. Then you can put your [medical] sleeve back on, and it holds it against your body so it not flopping around. Surprisingly, I’ve managed to sleep okay with it.

When I shower it has to stay completely dry. They give you a nice shower bag. CTV News - How important was it to have supportive medical staff help you through the process of having the Picc inserted? Peloza - Agnes was great.

She walked me through the process. Everything’s made sterile when you’re having it put in, and they actually cover you with fabric, including your face. That can be intimidating, [but] Agnes made it into a little tent so I wasn’t claustrophobic in there.

Then [she] had verbal instructions as you went through it. ‘I’m doing this.’ ‘The next part is going to feel like pressure for five seconds.’ Not everyone has good communication skills and it really helps when you are going through that process.

It is intimidating [and] a little bit scary. CTV News - What factors do you consider when making your healthcare decisions? Peloza - You’re making what you believe is the best call for your health based on the information you’re given by doctors and nurses.

stories.title: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza: Healing in the public eye
stories.summary: Following her first chemotherapy treatment, Peloza is sharing her healing journey in an ongoing series on CTV News at 6 p.m. and at CTVNewsLondon.CA
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
In January, London Coun. Elizabeth Peloza announced she had recently undergone surgery for breast cancer. Following her first chemotherapy treatment, Peloza is sharing her healing journey in an ongoing series on CTV News at 6 p.m. and at CTVNewsLondon.CA IN Photos: Navigating Cancer, Work, and Life On Friday March 6, Peloza invited a camera to film a visit to her family’s hairdresser at Candice B Artistry, as she decided to cut her shoulder-length hair very short in preparation for the coming weeks.

Viewers are invited to share feedback and questions at this email address, AskCTVLondon@bellmedia.CA, and CTV News will share the best with Peloza in a future interview. A conversation with Coun. Peloza CTV News- Why is this visit to your hairdresser different than previous visits?

Peloza - I’ve been blessed that Candice has been my family hair stylist for 14 years. She saw my kids grow up. She’s been the one to do their graduation pictures. She’s done my hair for inauguration pictures at City Hall.

This haircut really wasn’t a choice. It was a necessity. I know my hair is going to be gone in a couple of weeks. I’ve been reading about when to cut it, how to cut it, when to shave it. I know a lot of people don’t feel the hair loss, the tingling in the scalp like you left hair dye on for too long, until after their second chemotherapy treatment.

But mine has already started feeling irritated, so I’m just trying to be proactive. Emotionally, I’d rather wake up to a couple inches of hair on my pillow versus an entire handful. I’m just trying to do it now by choice versus waking up in sadness in a pile of hair.

CTV News - Some people go through chemotherapy privately. Why are you choosing to be more open about it? Peloza - I hope that people are proactive and get their testing done. Book your mammograms. Since the last news coverage, a lot of people are reaching out.

They’ve never had one done. They’re afraid to have one done. They’re afraid to find out what it might mean, what the results might be, but it’s more scary not to have a chance to fight because you waited too long. I’m hoping that we can destigmatize what it is to have cancer.

What it is to go through chemo, trying to find those good days. CTV News - This is happening on International Women’s Day. You said this has made you think about the intersection of hair and femininity. Tell me about that.

Peloza - Yes, it’s interesting that so many men are bald. They’ve shaved it [or] they’ve gone bald, and it’s like, oh, he’s still handsome. But that same beauty standard doesn’t really seem to extend to women. What Candice does [with my hair], I would probably never have picked, but [I’m] still excited to see what it looks like .

And it’ll grow back. It’s still just hair, but absolutely. So many people identify with hair as a part of their identity. CTV News- What feedback have you received from the public since you announced that you had surgery for breast cancer?

Peloza - A lot of support, a lot of people scheduling some of those (mammogram) appointments, or at least contemplating scheduling those appointments. Some residents are really supportive. Some expect business as usual. They have issues and you’re their representative.

CTV News - How have you prepared for chemotherapy given your role as Ward 12 City Councillor and City of London Budget Chair? Peloza - Really just making sure those relationships with staff are strong. Making sure they know where I’m at and when I’m handing things off to make sure they know why they’re helping take the lead on something, or responding to residents directly.

As for residents, I still have two events coming up that are scheduled. My newsletter is coming out soon, so just making sure that residents know I’m still here, but in-person I’m going to look quite different in my engagement.

Sending more texts versus phone calls because I’m fighting some issues with my esophagus. It’s already hurting and I’m having some trouble swallowing. It’s just discomfort, but ice cream seems to have been helping that. Really, it’s still business as usual.

Just business looks very different.

stories.title: Coun. Peloza reveals recent treatment for breast cancer
stories.summary: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has revealed she underwent surgery for breast cancer last month.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has revealed she underwent surgery for breast cancer last month. As Ward 12 councillor and budget chair, Peloza is widely respected by her colleagues at city hall for her work ethic, compassion, and candor.

So it isn’t surprising that she spoke bluntly about her recent diagnosis to CTV News on Friday. “Breast cancer. Didn’t see it coming. Haven’t been a smoker [and] used to run full marathons to raise money for charity. I was just doing a self-exam and thought I felt something,” she recalled.

Peloza underwent breast cancer surgery in December, only days after chairing budget deliberations at city hall. She used the holiday period to recover at home but still made it out to a community skate that she sponsored in her ward.

“Feeling really good. Surgery was last month. Healing is going exceptionally well for that,” she said. Subsequent test results have been clear, but she acknowledges there is still a journey ahead. “There’s going to be a treatment plan involving radiation for sure.

If chemo is on the table, I don’t know. I’ll wait for the doctors to give me that information and I will follow it,” Peloza explained. She is the chair of three council committees, and sits on several external agencies, boards, and commissions including Tourism London.

The mother of three has represented Ward 12 since 2018 and still intends to seek re-election later this year. “We might just see a little difference in door to door canvasing, maybe a few more ice cream socials where residents on the street come to me, or a neighbour can host me rather than going to people at each door,” Peloza explained.

“And if you think there’s something wrong, don’t shy away from it.”
